title: What you need
description: What Flexarr is, what kind of computer can run it, and whether you need Sonarr, Radarr and Lidarr.
headings: Do you need Sonarr, Radarr and Lidarr?
text: Flexarr comes in two halves. The server runs on a computer in your home and keeps your films, TV shows, music and podcasts. The apps on your iPhone, iPad, Apple TV and web browser connect to it and play from it. There's no account and no cloud service in the middle: your library stays on your own disk. If you've installed the iPhone app and it sent you here, this is the part you're missing. Set up the server once, then connect your phone to it with a short code. Flexarr is free for personal and other noncommercial use under the PolyForm Noncommercial licence. #A computer that stays on The server needs a machine that's switched on whenever you want to watch. Any of these work: A Mac, Apple silicon or Intel. Flexarr runs on it natively and uses the Mac's graphics chip to convert video. A NAS that runs containers, such as a Synology or an Unraid server. A Linux box or mini PC with Docker. That includes a Raspberry Pi 5 running a 64-bit operating system. A Windows PC with Docker Desktop. The Docker image is built for both 64-bit Intel/AMD (amd64) and 64-bit ARM (arm64) processors. There's no 32-bit build, and no native Windows or Linux download: on those, Docker is the way in. #Disk space Your media takes whatever it takes. Flexarr itself needs room for its database and a cache of artwork, subtitles, scrubbing previews and video it's converting at the moment. Leave a few gigabytes free on the drive that holds Flexarr's settings folder, more for a large library. #Processor and hardware transcoding Most of the time Flexarr sends files as they are. The iPhone, iPad and Apple TV apps play files directly by default, HDR and Dolby Vision included, so the server does little more than read from disk. The server converts (transcodes) video when a device can't play a file as it is: a web browser meeting a format it doesn't know, a stream limited to a lower quality for watching away from home, or some downloads. Converting is hard work for a processor, so this is where the machine matters: On a Mac, Flexarr uses Apple VideoToolbox automatically. Any recent Mac copes well. In Docker, Flexarr converts on the processor unless you choose hardware acceleration in Settings › Streaming, which lists only what the server's FFmpeg supports. See your platform's install page for what's available there. A modest machine is fine if you mostly watch on Apple devices at home. If you plan to stream to browsers or over a slow connection a lot, a faster processor (or a Mac) helps. Flexarr converts at most three videos at once by default and tells anyone beyond that the server is busy, rather than slowing everybody down. #Do you need Sonarr, Radarr and Lidarr? Flexarr is built to sit alongside Sonarr (TV), Radarr (films), Lidarr (music) and Seerr (requests). It doesn't download anything itself, and it takes its titles, artwork and details from those apps rather than asking you for API keys to online databases. You can run Flexarr without them, but what you get differs by library. Library With the app Without it Films Radarr supplies titles, posters, backgrounds, overviews, genres, ratings, trailers and cast. Films Radarr doesn't manage are looked up through its search. Films are found and play, named from their folders and files. Artwork and details come from any .nfo file and images (poster.jpg, fanart.jpg) in the film's folder, or from TMDB with a free key of your own. TV shows Sonarr supplies show and episode details and artwork. Flexarr adds cast from TVmaze. Episodes are found and play, organised from names like S01E02. Artwork and details come from any tvshow.nfo, episode .nfo files and images (poster.jpg, season01-poster.jpg, -thumb.jpg) beside them, or from TVmaze, which needs no setup. Music Lidarr adds artist pictures, album details and sorts albums, EPs and singles apart. Works well: Flexarr reads the tags in your files and uses cover.jpg or folder.jpg images, or art embedded in the files. Requests Seerr lets you search for and request films and show

title: Install on a Mac
description: Build Flexarr from source and run it natively on a Mac as a background service, with hardware video conversion through VideoToolbox.
headings: If your *arrs run in Docker on this Mac
text: On a Mac, Flexarr runs natively rather than in Docker. That way it can use the Mac's graphics hardware (Apple VideoToolbox) to convert video, which Docker on macOS can't. It works on Apple silicon and Intel Macs. There's no downloadable Mac app or installer yet. You build Flexarr from its source code with one command, which installs it as a background service that starts when you log in. It takes some time in Terminal, but you only do it once. Note Prefer not to build anything? Docker Desktop for Mac runs the Docker image too, but without VideoToolbox: video is converted on the processor. #Before you start You'll build on one Mac and install on another over SSH. They can be the same Mac, which is what this page assumes. You need: macOS command line tools (git, make, Python). Run xcode-select --install in Terminal, or install Xcode. Homebrew, for FFmpeg and Node.js. The .NET 10 SDK, from Microsoft's download page. Choose the latest SDK installer for your Mac (Arm64 for Apple silicon, x64 for Intel). Node.js 24 or later: brew install node. FFmpeg, on the Mac that will run Flexarr: brew install ffmpeg. Flexarr uses it to read your files and convert video. #Turn on Remote Login The install script copies Flexarr into place and starts it over SSH, even on the same Mac. Open System Settings › General › Sharing and turn on Remote Login. In Terminal, make an SSH key if you don't have one, and let it sign in to this Mac without a password: ssh-keygen -t ed25519 # press Return to accept the defaults ssh-copy-id localhost ssh localhost true # should finish without asking for a password #Build and install Get the source code: git clone https://github.com/danleach-glitch/flexarr.git cd flexarr Build and install: make deploy DEPLOY_HOST=localhost The script builds the web app and the server, downloads Microsoft's ASP.NET Core runtime into ~/.dotnet (checking it against Microsoft's published checksum), copies Flexarr into ~/.flexarr, and starts it. It waits until Flexarr answers, then prints its address, something like http://your-mac.local:8383. To install on a different Mac, use its SSH host name in place of localhost, for example make deploy DEPLOY_HOST=mini. That Mac needs Remote Login and FFmpeg, but not the SDK or Node.js. #Where things live Path What's there ~/.flexarr/app Flexarr itself. Replaced each time you install. ~/.flexarr/data Your settings (config.json), database and caches. Installing never touches it. ~/.flexarr/logs Log files, one a day. console.log has errors from when the server couldn't start. ~/Library/LaunchAgents/io.github.flexarr.server.plist The service: starts Flexarr at login and restarts it if it stops. #Keep it running Flexarr runs as a LaunchAgent, which means it runs while you're logged in. On a Mac that acts as a server: Turn on automatic login for your user in System Settings › Users & Groups. (macOS doesn't offer it while FileVault is on.) Stop the Mac going to sleep on its own, in System Settings' energy or battery settings. To restart, stop or start Flexarr by hand: launchctl kickstart -k gui/$(id -u)/io.github.flexarr.server # restart launchctl bootout gui/$(id -u)/io.github.flexarr.server # stop launchctl bootstrap gui/$(id -u) ~/Library/LaunchAgents/io.github.flexarr.server.plist # start #Media on an external drive The first time Flexarr reads a library on an external drive, macOS may ask whether to allow access. Allow it. If scans can't see your media, look in System Settings › Privacy & Security under Files & Folders (or Full Disk Access) for dotnet, the program Flexarr runs under, and turn its access on. #Hardware transcoding Nothing to set up. Settings › Streaming › Hardware acceleration starts on Automatic, which on a Mac means Apple VideoToolbox. The graphics hardware decodes H.264 and HEVC; other formats (older AVI files, VC-1 and the like) are decoded on the processor and still encoded in hardware. #If your *arrs run in Docker on this Mac Sonarr, Radarr and Lidarr in Docker see your media unde

title: Install on a Synology NAS
description: Run Flexarr on a Synology NAS as a Container Manager project, with its settings folder, your media and the right permissions.
text: On a Synology NAS, Flexarr runs as a container in Container Manager, Synology's Docker app. You need DSM 7.2 or later and a model that supports Container Manager. Flexarr's image is built for both Intel/AMD and 64-bit ARM processors, so if Container Manager installs on your model, Flexarr should run. #1. Install Container Manager Open Package Center, search for Container Manager and install it. Installing it creates a shared folder called docker. #2. Make the folders Container Manager won't create missing folders for you, so make them first in File Station: In the docker shared folder, create a folder called flexarr. Inside it, create a folder called config. This holds Flexarr's settings, database and caches. Note where your media is, for example /volume1/data/media with movies, tv and music inside. If you run Sonarr, Radarr and Lidarr on the NAS, use the folder they use. #3. Find your user ID You tell the Flexarr container which user to run as, with PUID and PGID, so it can write to its folder and read your media. You need that user's numeric ID and group ID. In Control Panel › Terminal & SNMP, tick Enable SSH service and apply. From a computer, connect with ssh yourname@your-nas and run id: id # uid=1026(yourname) gid=100(users) ... Note the two numbers (here 1026 and 100). You can turn SSH off again afterwards. Tip Use an account that can read your media shares and write to the docker share. If your *arrs already run with a PUID and PGID, use those same numbers. #4. Create the project Open Container Manager and go to Project, then Create. Project name: flexarr. Path: choose Set path and pick docker/flexarr. Source: choose Create docker-compose.yml and paste this, changing the IDs and the media path to yours: services: flexarr: image: ghcr.io/danleach-glitch/flexarr:latest container_name: flexarr environment: [PUID=1026, PGID=100] ports: ["8383:8383"] volumes: - /volume1/docker/flexarr/config:/config - /volume1/data/media:/data/media restart: unless-stopped Click Next. You can skip the web portal settings. Click Next again, then Done. Container Manager downloads the image and starts Flexarr. The project shows as running when it's ready. #About the media path Mount your media at the same path inside the container that Sonarr, Radarr and Lidarr use inside theirs. If they all see /data/media/tv/..., the paths they report to Flexarr match what Flexarr sees and everything lines up. If they don't, you can map one to the other in Settings › Connections › Media folders. See Media paths. #Port Flexarr listens on port 8383. If you use DSM's firewall (Control Panel › Security › Firewall), allow that port from your home network. #Hardware transcoding Flexarr converts video on the processor by default. Many Intel-based Synology models have a graphics chip that can do this work, and the Flexarr image includes the Intel drivers. If your NAS has /dev/dri (check with ls /dev/dri over SSH), add this to the service in the project's docker-compose.yml: devices: - /dev/dri:/dev/dri Then choose Intel Quick Sync or VA-API (Intel and AMD on Linux) in Settings › Streaming › Hardware acceleration and play something that needs converting. If it fails, set it back to Automatic. This matters less than you might expect: the iPhone, iPad and Apple TV apps play most files directly, so the server only converts for web browsers, quality-limited streams away from home and some downloads. On a NAS with a low-power processor, keep those to one or two at a time. #Updating When a new release is out, Container Manager's Image page marks the Flexarr image as having an update. Select it and choose Update, and Container Manager restarts Flexarr on the new version. Your settings stay in docker/flexarr/config. See Updating. #Next: set it up In Container Manager, select the container and open Log. It says Set it up at http://localhost:8383/#setup=…. title: Install on Unraid
description: Add Flexarr to Unraid as a Docker container by hand, with its appdata folder, your media share and the right user.
text: On Unraid, Flexarr runs as a Docker container. There's no Community Applications template for it yet, so you add the container by hand. It takes a few minutes and you only do it once. #Before you start Make sure Docker is enabled, under Settings › Docker. Know where your media lives, for example the data share at /mnt/user/data/media. If you run Sonarr, Radarr and Lidarr on this server, look at the media path in their containers' settings: you'll give Flexarr the same one. #Add the container Go to the Docker tab and click Add Container at the bottom of the page. Fill in the top of the form: Name: flexarr Repository: ghcr.io/danleach-glitch/flexarr:latest Network Type: Host, so the Apple TV and iPhone apps find Flexarr by themselves. Bridge works too, but then you type the server's address in the apps. Switch the form to the advanced view with the Basic View toggle at the top right, and fill in: WebUI: http://[IP]:[PORT:8383]/ Add the port, the settings folder, your media and the user to run as with Add another Path, Port, Variable, Label or Device at the bottom, one at a time: Config Type Name Container Host Port Web UI 8383 8383 Path Config /config /mnt/user/appdata/flexarr Path Media /data/media /mnt/user/data/media Variable PUID PUID 99 Variable PGID PGID 100 Change the media paths to match yours. The container path should be the one your *arrs use inside their containers. Click Apply. Unraid downloads the image and starts Flexarr. #Why PUID 99 and PGID 100 They run Flexarr as Unraid's usual nobody:users, the owner of files on your shares and in appdata, so it can write its settings and read your media. If your other containers use a different PUID and PGID, use those numbers instead. Flexarr gives appdata/flexarr to that user when it starts. #Media paths Sonarr, Radarr and Lidarr tell Flexarr where each new file is. When all of them see your media at the same container path (here /data/media), those paths match and new downloads appear straight away. If they don't, map one to the other in Settings › Connections › Media folders. See Media paths. #Hardware transcoding Flexarr converts video on the processor by default. On Linux, Settings › Streaming › Hardware acceleration › Automatic means the processor. Intel and AMD graphics. The image includes the drivers. Edit the container and add a Device with /dev/dri as its value, then apply. VA-API (Intel and AMD on Linux), and on Intel Intel Quick Sync, appear in Settings › Streaming. Choose one and play something that needs converting. If it fails, set it back to Automatic. NVIDIA graphics may work, because Unraid's NVIDIA driver supplies the libraries to the container. This is untested, so treat it as an experiment: Install the Nvidia Driver plugin from the Apps tab and reboot if it asks. Edit the Flexarr container. Add --runtime=nvidia to Extra Parameters. Add two Variables: NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES set to all (or your card's ID from the plugin's page), and NVIDIA_DRIVER_CAPABILITIES set to compute,video,utility. Apply, then choose NVIDIA NVENC in Settings › Streaming and play something that needs converting. If it fails, set it back to Automatic. Note Conversion matters less than you might think. The iPhone, iPad and Apple TV apps play most files directly, so the server mainly converts for web browsers, quality-limited streams away from home and some downloads. #Updating The Docker tab shows when a newer Flexarr image is available. Click apply update under the container to move to it. Your settings stay in appdata/flexarr. See Updating. #Next: set it up Click Flexarr's icon in the Docker tab and choose Logs. It says Set it up at http://localhost:8383/#setup=…. Copy that link into a browser on your home network, putting your Unraid server's name or IP address in place of localhost. The page has the setup code filled in, so you only choose a PIN and choose Set up Flexarr: the first browser to do it becomes the new server's owner. title: Install with Docker on Linux or Windows
description: Run Flexarr's Docker image on a Linux machine, or on Windows through Docker Desktop and WSL 2, with docker run or Docker Compose.
text: On Linux and Windows, Flexarr runs as a Docker container. The image is ghcr.io/danleach-glitch/flexarr, built for 64-bit Intel/AMD (amd64) and 64-bit ARM (arm64), so it also runs on a Raspberry Pi 5 with a 64-bit operating system. There's no native Windows build: on Windows, use Docker Desktop. #What the container needs Inside the container What to give it Port 8383 Publish it as 8383 on the host. Settings /config A folder (or Docker volume) for Flexarr's settings, database and caches. Keep it: it's your whole setup. Media /data/media (your choice) Your media folder. Mount it at the same path Sonarr, Radarr and Lidarr use, so the paths they report match what Flexarr sees. The latest tag is always the newest release. To upgrade only when you choose, use a version instead, such as ghcr.io/danleach-glitch/flexarr:0.49. #Linux #Permissions Flexarr runs as user ID 1654 unless you tell it otherwise. It needs to write to its settings folder and read your media, so the simplest way is to run it as the user who owns your media with PUID and PGID, as with Sonarr, Radarr and Lidarr. Find your IDs with id: id # uid=1000(you) gid=1000(you) ... When it starts, Flexarr gives its settings folder to that user, so it doesn't matter if Docker created the folder as root. Note Docker's --user option (user: in Compose) works too, in place of PUID and PGID. The container then changes no owners, so create the settings folder yourself first (mkdir -p ~/flexarr/config) so it belongs to you. #docker run docker run -d --name flexarr --restart unless-stopped \ -e PUID=1000 -e PGID=1000 \ -p 8383:8383 \ -v ~/flexarr/config:/config \ -v /path/to/media:/data/media \ ghcr.io/danleach-glitch/flexarr:latest Tip You can keep the settings in a named Docker volume instead, with -v flexarr-config:/config. #Docker Compose Save this as docker-compose.yml and run docker compose up -d in the same folder. services: flexarr: image: ghcr.io/danleach-glitch/flexarr:latest container_name: flexarr environment: [PUID=1000, PGID=1000] ports: ["8383:8383"] volumes: - ./config:/config - /path/to/media:/data/media restart: unless-stopped If Sonarr, Radarr and Lidarr are in the same Compose file, give them the same media mount (/path/to/media:/data/media). They can then reach Flexarr at http://flexarr:8383 for webhooks. #Found on your network The Apple TV, iPhone and iPad list servers that announce themselves on the Wi-Fi. Docker's own network doesn't pass the announcement on, so to have Flexarr listed, run it on the host's network: --network host in place of -p 8383:8383 with docker run, or in Compose: network_mode: host in place of the ports: line. Flexarr is then at port 8383 on the computer itself. Without it, everything still works; in the apps, choose Enter an address instead and type http://<server>:8383. Note On the host's network, other containers in the Compose file can't reach Flexarr as http://flexarr:8383. Use the computer's address instead, or http://host.docker.internal:8383 with extra_hosts: ["host.docker.internal:host-gateway"] on those containers. #Hardware transcoding Flexarr converts video on the processor unless you pick something else in Settings › Streaming › Hardware acceleration. On Linux, Automatic means the processor. The menu lists only what the container can use. The Apple apps play most files directly, so many homes rarely need conversion at all. Intel and AMD graphics. The image includes the VA-API drivers: AMD's on both amd64 and arm64, Intel's (with Quick Sync) on amd64 only. Pass the graphics device into the container, with --device /dev/dri for docker run or this under the service in Compose: devices: - /dev/dri:/dev/dri Flexarr joins the device's group by itself. Then VA-API (Intel and AMD on Linux), and on Intel Intel Quick Sync, appear in Settings › Streaming. Choose one and play something that needs converting. If it fails, set it back to Automatic. title: First setup
description: Open your new Flexarr server in a browser, make yourself its owner, add your films, shows and music, and find the API key if you ever need it.
text: Once the server is installed and running, everything else happens in a web browser. There's no account to make and no key to copy: the first browser on your home network to enter the server's setup code becomes its owner. #Open Flexarr in a browser Flexarr listens on port 8383. On a computer on the same home network as the server, open: http://<server>:8383 Replace <server> with the server's address. Any of these usually work: On the server itself: http://localhost:8383 The server's name on your network, such as http://mac-mini.local:8383 Its IP address, such as http://192.168.1.20:8383. Your router's app or admin page lists the addresses of devices on your network. If the page doesn't load, check that Flexarr is running (your install guide, linked from What you need, shows how) and that you've typed http://, not https://. #Enter the setup code Usually there's nothing to look up: The Mac app opens the welcome page in your browser the first time it starts, with the code already filled in. Open Flexarr in its menu does the same until the server is set up. Docker (including Synology and Unraid): the container's log says Set it up at http://localhost:8383/#setup=…. Open that link. From another computer, put the server's name or IP address in place of localhost. Pasting the whole link into the setup code box works too. Either way you only choose a PIN. If you open the server's address without the link, it asks for the code itself. A new server greets you with Welcome to your Flexarr server and asks for its setup code. The code proves you're the one who installed it: some setups (a reverse proxy, Docker Desktop) make visitors from the internet look as though they're on your home network, and only someone with the server can read its code. It's eight letters and numbers, like K7QM-3PXT, and it's in: Docker (including Synology and Unraid): the container's log. Run docker logs flexarr, or open the container's log in your NAS's Docker app. It's also in setup-code.txt in the container's settings folder. The Mac app: the menu bar menu, as Setup Code. Choose it to copy the code. macOS (installed with the script): ~/.flexarr/logs/console.log, or ~/.flexarr/data/setup-code.txt. Type it in, choose a PIN to protect the server's settings (4 to 8 digits, typed twice), and choose Set up Flexarr. This browser becomes the server's owner and is signed in. That's the whole sign-up. Watching doesn't need the PIN; changing settings does. If you close the page before choosing Set up Flexarr, nothing has happened yet, and the same code still works. The code stops working once the server is set up, and after ten wrong tries it's replaced with a new one (the log says so). A few things to know: It only works once. As soon as anyone signs in, setup closes for good. Every other phone, tablet, TV and browser then connects with a code that you approve from this browser. See Connect your devices. It only works from home. The button appears only to a browser on your home network, reaching the server by its IP address, a .local name or the server's own name. That stops anyone on the internet, or a web page you happen to visit, from claiming your server. Servers set up before version 0.49.0 aren't affected. They keep using the API key, as before. Note If you see a box asking for an API key instead of the welcome, someone has already set this server up, or you're not on the home network. Try opening it by its IP address from a computer at home. If you set it up yourself in another browser, approve this one from there with a code, or sign in with the key (see The API key below). #The setup guide Next, Flexarr welcomes you with a short setup guide, one card at a time. Choose Get started, or I'll set it up myself to go straight to Home. Every step after your name can be skipped, and Set up later leaves the guide whenever you like: Your name. title: Without Sonarr and Radarr
description: Artwork and details for films and shows that Sonarr and Radarr don't manage, from the files beside them, TVmaze and TMDB, and home video libraries.
headings: Artwork and .nfo files in your folders
text: Flexarr works best alongside Sonarr and Radarr, but it doesn't need them. Films and shows they don't manage, or every film and show if you don't run them, get their artwork and details in three ways, best first: What's in their folders. A .nfo file and artwork beside a film or show always win, even over Sonarr's and Radarr's. TVmaze, for shows. It needs no account or key. TMDB, for films, with a free key of your own. Anything none of these find still plays, named from its folder and files. #Artwork and .nfo files in your folders If you've used Kodi, Jellyfin, Emby, Plex or tinyMediaManager, your folders may already hold everything Flexarr needs. Flexarr reads: What Where Details (title, year, plot, genres, rating, age rating, IDs) movie.nfo (or Film name.nfo) beside a film, tvshow.nfo in a show's folder, Episode name.nfo beside an episode Poster poster.jpg, folder.jpg or cover.jpg Background fanart.jpg, backdrop.jpg or background.jpg Logo clearlogo.png or logo.png Season poster season01-poster.jpg (or season-specials-poster.jpg) in the show's folder, or poster.jpg in the season's folder Episode still Episode name-thumb.jpg or Episode name.jpg beside the episode A film on its own in the library's folder, rather than in a folder of its own, uses the same names with its file name in front: Heat (1995)-poster.jpg, Heat (1995)-fanart.jpg. Images can be JPEG, PNG or WebP. Flexarr only reads these files: it never writes or changes anything in your media folders. Tip The IDs in a .nfo file (TMDB, IMDb or TheTVDB) help Flexarr find exactly the right title, in Sonarr and Radarr as well as online. A .nfo that holds only a link to the title's IMDb or TMDB page works too. #Shows from TVmaze Shows Sonarr doesn't know are looked up on TVmaze, by the show's folder name (and its IDs, when there are any). They get a poster, background, overview, genres, rating and cast, with episode titles, descriptions and stills. There's nothing to set up. #Films from TMDB For films Radarr doesn't know, Flexarr can ask TMDB, using a key of your own: Sign up at themoviedb.org (it's free) and open Settings › API. Ask for a key. TMDB asks you to register an application first; that's the form for everyone, not something only developers do: Choose personal (non-commercial) use. Application name: something like Flexarr at home. Application URL: your Flexarr's address, or https://flexarr.io. Application summary: something like My own media server, showing details and artwork for films I own. Fill in your contact details and accept the terms. The key appears straight away. In Flexarr, open Settings › Connections, choose Connect on TMDB, and paste the API key or the API read access token. Choose Test, then Save. Films that weren't matched are looked up again straight away. They get a poster, background, logo, overview, genres, age rating, rating, trailer and cast. #When the match is wrong A title search can pick the wrong one: a remake, or an older show of the same name. Titles matched by searching are listed under Check these matches in Library health. To choose the right one, open the title, choose Fix match… in its ⋯ menu, and search. Without Sonarr and Radarr, the search is TVmaze's (shows) or TMDB's (films), and your choice is kept in Flexarr through every refresh. Fixing a film's match without Radarr needs a TMDB key. #Home videos For videos of your own, add a library of the kind Home videos in Settings › Libraries. Nothing in it is looked up online. Flexarr arranges it by folder: Each folder in the library's folder is shown like a show. The folders inside that are its seasons, named after the folders. Any folders deeper down are part of the season they're in. Each video is an episode, named after its file. Folders and videos are in name order, with numbers counted as numbers, so Part 2 comes before Part 10. Name them by date (2019-07 Cornwall) to keep them in date order. Videos straight in a show's folder come first, and videos straight in the library's folder

title: Connect your devices
description: Connect an iPhone, iPad, Apple TV or another browser to your Flexarr server with a short code, and manage the devices signed in to it.
headings: If the app can't find your server
text: Every device signs in to your server with a code. The device shows the code, and you allow it: on an iPhone or Android phone that's already signed in to Flexarr as the main profile, which asks you by itself, or on the computer where you set up Flexarr. Each device then gets a sign-in of its own, which you can rename or sign out at any time. #Allow it from your phone When a device asks to connect, every iPhone and Android phone signed in as the main profile asks Connect “Living room”?, with the device's code. Check the code matches the one on the device's screen and tap Allow. If the device isn't yours, tap Don't allow: the device says Not allowed, and asks again only if someone there chooses Try again. The phone asks while Flexarr is open on it. When it isn't, a notification says the device wants to connect, if notifications are turned on for that phone. Choose Allow or Don't allow on the notification itself (the phone asks to be unlocked first), or tap it to get the same question in the app. The web app asks too, when it's open on the main profile. To see every device waiting, open Settings in the app, or Settings › Security › Connect a device on the web. Each one has Allow and Don't allow. Turned a device away by mistake? Choose Try again on the device, and allow it this time. (An app from before version 0.56 shows a new code by itself instead; you aren't asked about that one, but it's listed in Settings as turned away, with Allow.) #iPhone and iPad Get the app from the App Store. The first time you open it, three short cards explain what Flexarr is, that it plays from your own Flexarr server at home, and how it finds that server on your Wi-Fi. If you haven't set up a server yet, Set up at flexarr.io brings you to this guide. If you have, choose Skip, or Next through to Find my server. When iOS asks whether Flexarr can find devices on your local network, choose Allow. Without it, the app can't see your server. Under Servers on your network, choose your server. The app shows Connect this iPhone (or iPad) with a code like ABC-123. On another phone signed in to Flexarr, tap Allow when it asks (see Allow it from your phone). Or, on your computer, open the server's address in a browser, go to Settings › Security › Connect a device, type in the code and choose Continue. Check that the code matches the one on your phone, and choose Allow. The app moves on by itself a moment later. If your household has several profiles, it asks who's watching. If Safari on the same phone is already signed in to Flexarr, Approve in Safari instead opens the approval page there, so you don't need the computer. #Apple TV The Apple TV app isn't on the App Store yet. Until it is, install it with Xcode. Open Flexarr on the Apple TV. It lists Servers on your network; choose yours. The TV shows Connect this Apple TV and a code. On your phone, tap Allow when it asks, checking the code matches. Or, on your computer, go to Settings › Security › Connect a device, type in the code, then choose Continue and Allow. The TV also shows a QR code. Scan it with a phone that's already signed in to Flexarr in its browser, and the approval page opens with the code filled in. Note A code lasts as long as the device keeps showing it. If you go back and choose the server again, the device gets a new code. #Other browsers Browsers don't get a code. Open the server's address in the new browser and it asks for the API key: type it in once, and the browser gets a sign-in of its own, so it doesn't keep the key. Over Tailscale, browsers sign in by your Tailscale account instead, with no key. #Who can approve a device Only the main profile can connect devices. title: Install the Apple TV app with Xcode
description: Build the Flexarr Apple TV app from source and install it on your own Apple TV with a Mac and Xcode, until it arrives on the App Store.
headings: 2. Sign Xcode in to your Apple ID
3. Pair the Apple TV with your Mac
text: The Flexarr Apple TV app is coming to the App Store. Until it's there, you can build it yourself and install it on your own Apple TV with a Mac. It takes about half an hour the first time, most of it downloading Xcode. If you only want Flexarr on an iPhone or iPad, you don't need any of this: that app is on the App Store. #What you need A Mac that can run Xcode 26 or later. Xcode 26 or later, free from the Mac App Store. Open it once after installing, and when it offers to download platforms, include tvOS. (If you skipped that, add it later in Xcode › Settings › Components.) XcodeGen, which makes the Xcode project from the files in the repository. With Homebrew: brew install xcodegen. Git, to download the source. macOS offers to install it the first time you type git in Terminal. An Apple ID. A free one works. An Apple TV running tvOS 18.2 or later, on the same network as the Mac. Important With a free Apple ID, apps you install yourself stop opening after 7 days. Run the install command again to renew it for another week; your settings and sign-in are kept. A paid Apple Developer Program membership makes installs last a year. #1. Download the source In Terminal: git clone https://github.com/danleach-glitch/flexarr.git cd flexarr #2. Sign Xcode in to your Apple ID Open Xcode, then Xcode › Settings › Accounts, choose + and sign in with your Apple ID. Xcode makes a free "Personal Team" for it. #Find your Team ID The install command needs your team's ID, a 10-character code like A1B2C3D4E5. Paid membership: it's on developer.apple.com/account under Membership details. Free Apple ID: Xcode makes a development certificate for you the first time it signs an app (or when you choose Manage Certificates… › + › Apple Development in Xcode › Settings › Accounts). The Team ID is the certificate's organisational unit. In Terminal: security find-certificate -c "Apple Development" -p | openssl x509 -noout -subject The Team ID is the value after OU=. #3. Pair the Apple TV with your Mac On the Apple TV, open Settings › Remotes and Devices › Remote App and Devices. Leave this screen open. On the Mac, in Xcode, open Window › Devices and Simulators (⇧⌘2). Your Apple TV appears under Discovered. Select it and choose Pair. Type the code the TV shows into Xcode. Pairing only happens once. Xcode may take a few minutes to get the Apple TV ready the first time. #4. Build and install Choose a bundle ID: a reverse-domain name that's yours, such as com.yourname.flexarr.tv. Apple needs every app's ID to be unique, so don't use one that belongs to someone else. Then, in the flexarr folder: make apple-install TEAM=A1B2C3D4E5 BUNDLE_ID=com.yourname.flexarr.tv This generates the Xcode project, builds the app, signs it with your team, installs it on the first paired Apple TV it finds and opens it. With more than one Apple TV, name the one you want with DEVICE= and its identifier, shown in Xcode's Devices and Simulators window: make apple-install TEAM=A1B2C3D4E5 BUNDLE_ID=com.yourname.flexarr.tv DEVICE=<identifier> The first build takes several minutes. When Flexarr opens on the TV, connect it to your server. #Updating the app Download the latest source and run the same command again: git pull make apple-install TEAM=A1B2C3D4E5 BUNDLE_ID=com.yourname.flexarr.tv Use the same bundle ID every time, so the TV treats it as the same app and keeps your sign-in. Keeping the app and the server on the same version avoids surprises; see Updating. #Troubleshooting #"No paired Apple TV found" The Mac can't see a paired Apple TV. Check both are on the same network, the Apple TV is awake, and it's listed (and connected) in Xcode's Devices and Simulators window. If it's listed but greyed out, wake the TV and wait a minute. #xcodegen: command not found Install XcodeGen (brew install xcodegen), then open a new Terminal window. #Signing errors: "No Account for Team", "No profiles were found" Check the TEAM value is your Team ID, not your email address or name, and that Xcode is sig

title: Updating Flexarr
description: How to update the Flexarr server in Docker or on a Mac, what happens to your data when you do, and how to keep the apps up to date.
headings: Keeping the apps up to date
text: Updating Flexarr replaces the program and leaves your data alone. Your settings, profiles, watch history and libraries live in the data folder (/config in Docker, ~/.flexarr/data on a Mac), which an update never overwrites. #Before you update Read what's changed. Every release is listed, newest first, in: Settings › About on your server, under What's new the changelog GitHub releases Settings › Updates shows the version you're running now and the newest release, with what's changed in it. #Settings › Updates Flexarr asks GitHub once a day whether there's a newer release, and Settings shows a dot beside Updates when there is. To look straight away, choose Check for updates. The check sends nothing about your server but its version. What happens next depends on how you installed Flexarr: On a Mac (installed with the install script), choose Update now. Flexarr downloads the new version, checks it against the checksum published with the release, brings the .NET runtime up to date if it needs to, and restarts to install it, which takes a minute or two. If anything is playing, being watched live or recording, it asks first, because the restart interrupts it. In Docker, a container can't replace itself, so the page shows the commands to update it (see Docker below). Anything else, such as running from source, is updated the way you installed it. #Automatic updates on a Mac Turn on Install updates automatically to have a Mac install update itself. It's off unless you turn it on. Flexarr installs a new release between 4 and 5 in the morning, after the nightly backup, and only when nothing is playing, being watched live or recording. A busy night waits for the next. A release that failed to install isn't tried again by itself; you can still install it with Update now. #If an update doesn't start Before swapping in the new version, Flexarr copies the database aside. If the new version doesn't answer within five minutes, the version you had is put back, with the database as it was, and Settings › Updates says what happened. The update's own log is ~/.flexarr/logs/update.log, and the version that didn't start is kept in ~/.flexarr/app.failed so you can report what went wrong. The version before the last successful update is kept in ~/.flexarr/app.previous. Each update also brings the .NET runtime Flexarr runs on (in ~/.dotnet) up to its latest patch, as the install script does, so your server gets Microsoft's security fixes. The download is checked against the checksum Microsoft publishes. If it can't be fetched, the update carries on with the runtime you have, unless the new version needs a newer one. You don't need to make a backup by hand: Flexarr makes one itself whenever an update is about to change the database (see below). If you'd like an extra copy anyway, choose Back up now in Settings › Backup and restore. #Docker Flexarr's image is ghcr.io/danleach-glitch/flexarr. Updating means downloading the newer image and making a new container from it, with the same settings and folders as before. #With Docker Compose In the folder with your docker-compose.yml: docker compose pull flexarr docker compose up -d flexarr Compose replaces the container only if the image has changed. #With docker run Download the new image, remove the old container, and start a new one with the same command you used to install: docker pull ghcr.io/danleach-glitch/flexarr:latest docker stop flexarr docker rm flexarr docker run -d --name flexarr \ -p 8383:8383 \ -v /path/to/config:/config \ -v /path/to/media:/data/media \ ghcr.io/danleach-glitch/flexarr:latest Removing the container doesn't touch your data, as long as /config is a folder or volume you mounted. Use exactly the same -v paths as before. Note On a Synology or Unraid server, use the platform's own way to update a container. See Install on a Synology NAS or Install on Unraid. #Which tag to use Images are published for every release with these tags: Tag What it follows latest The newest release. Every u

title: Connect Sonarr, Radarr, Lidarr and Seerr
description: Add your *arr apps and Seerr to Flexarr for artwork, Coming soon, requests and instant imports, and set up webhooks so new downloads appear straight away.
headings: Webhooks: new downloads appear straight away
text: Flexarr is built to sit alongside Sonarr, Radarr, Lidarr and Seerr. It doesn't download anything itself; it takes its artwork and details from them, and they tell it when something new arrives. If you don't run them yet, Flexarr still plays your files. See What you need for what you get with and without each one. #What each connection gives you App What Flexarr gets from it Radarr Titles, posters, backgrounds, overviews, genres, ratings and trailers for films. Upcoming films in Coming soon. Deleting a film from Flexarr goes through Radarr. Film series for collections. Sonarr Show and episode details and artwork. Upcoming episodes in Coming soon. Deleting a show or episode goes through Sonarr. Lidarr Artist pictures, album covers, canonical names and years, and albums, EPs and singles sorted apart. Seerr Discover and requests. Seerr and Overseerr both work. See Requests. Bazarr Search for subtitles from the player and a title's page, and re-syncing subtitles that are out of time. See Finding subtitles. Films and shows that Radarr or Sonarr don't manage are still looked up through their search, so a connected Radarr fills in artwork even for films it didn't download. #Add a connection You need two things for each app: its address and its API key. In Flexarr, go to Settings › Connections. Every app Flexarr works with is listed under Apps & Integrations. Find the one you want and choose Connect. Type its Address, such as http://192.168.1.20:7878. Paste its API key. Choose Test. A tick means Flexarr reached it; otherwise you'll see what went wrong. Choose Connect. Repeat for each app. Each one then shows a green dot, its version, and a link to open it. Choose the pencil to change or remove it. If you run more than one Sonarr, Radarr or Lidarr, such as a second Radarr for 4K films, choose + beside the one already connected and give the new one a Name of its own, such as "Radarr 4K". #The address Use the address Flexarr can reach the app on, with its port. The usual ports are: App Usual address Sonarr http://<host>:8989 Radarr http://<host>:7878 Lidarr http://<host>:8686 Seerr http://<host>:5055 Bazarr http://<host>:6767 localhost only works if the app runs on the same machine as Flexarr and neither is in its own Docker container. Between containers, use the machine's IP address, or the container's name if they share a Docker network. #Where to find each API key App Where its API key is Sonarr Settings › General, under Security Radarr Settings › General, under Security Lidarr Settings › General, under Security Seerr Settings › General Bazarr Settings › General, under Security #Seerr Seerr has its own row under Apps. Choose the pencil beside Seerr, type its Address and API key, and choose Save. Once it's connected, Discover fills with what's trending and popular, and you can request what you don't have. See Requests. #Bazarr Bazarr has its own row too. Choose the pencil beside Bazarr, type its Address and API key, and choose Save. Bazarr needs Sonarr and Radarr connected on its side, at least one languages profile and some subtitle sites (providers); set those up in Bazarr itself. A title you search for gets Bazarr's first languages profile if it has none, so Bazarr's own schedule may then fetch subtitles for it too. See Finding subtitles. #Webhooks: new downloads appear straight away Without webhooks, Flexarr finds new files on its own scan every 12 hours. With them, Sonarr, Radarr and Lidarr tell Flexarr the moment they import, upgrade, rename or delete something, and Flexarr rescans only that folder. The addresses to use are at the bottom of Settings › Connections, under Webhooks, already filled in with your server's address and its webhook secret. They look like this: http://<flexarr-host>:8383/api/v1/webhooks/sonarr?secret=<webhook-secret> http://<flexarr-host>:8383/api/v1/webhooks/radarr?secret=<webhook-secret> http://<flexarr-host>:8383/api/v1/webhooks/lidarr?secret=<webhook-secret> The secret can only start scans, so you don't

title: Media paths
description: Why Flexarr needs to see your files at the same paths as Sonarr, Radarr and Lidarr, how to line them up in Docker, and how to use path mappings when you can't.
headings: The best fix: the same paths everywhere
When the paths can't match: path mappings
text: Sonarr, Radarr and Lidarr talk to Flexarr about files by their path. When Sonarr imports an episode, its webhook says "I've just put a file in /tv/Some Show/Season 1", and Flexarr rescans that folder. When you delete a film, Flexarr works out whether Radarr manages it by comparing paths. If Flexarr sees the same file somewhere else, say /data/media/tv/Some Show/Season 1, it can't tell they're the same folder. This mostly matters in Docker, where each container sees your disks at whatever paths its volumes give it. There are two ways to fix it: give every container the same paths (best), or tell Flexarr how to translate them. #The best fix: the same paths everywhere Mount your media at the same path in every container. A common layout is one parent folder, /data/media, with a folder for each kind: services: flexarr: image: ghcr.io/danleach-glitch/flexarr:latest ports: ["8383:8383"] volumes: - /srv/flexarr:/config - /srv/media:/data/media sonarr: image: lscr.io/linuxserver/sonarr:latest volumes: - /srv/sonarr:/config - /srv/media:/data/media radarr: image: lscr.io/linuxserver/radarr:latest volumes: - /srv/radarr:/config - /srv/media:/data/media lidarr: image: lscr.io/linuxserver/lidarr:latest volumes: - /srv/lidarr:/config - /srv/media:/data/media The left side (/srv/media) is where the media is on the host. The right side (/data/media) is where every container sees it. Because the right side is the same everywhere, a file is /data/media/tv/Some Show/… to all of them. Then use those paths everywhere: Root folders in Sonarr, Radarr and Lidarr: /data/media/tv, /data/media/movies, /data/media/music Library folders in Flexarr's Settings › Libraries: the same three Tip If your downloads folder is on the same disk, mount the parent of both (for example /srv/data:/data, with media and downloads inside) in the *arrs. That lets them move files instead of copying them. Flexarr only needs to see the media. #When the paths can't match: path mappings Sometimes you can't change the volumes, or the *arrs run in Docker and Flexarr runs natively on a Mac. Then add a path mapping: "what Sonarr calls this, Flexarr calls that". #In Settings Go to Settings › Connections and find Media folders. Each of Sonarr, Radarr and Lidarr's root folders has a line saying where it is on this server. Usually Flexarr works this out by itself. It compares the folders Sonarr, Radarr and Lidarr keep their shows, films and artists in with the folders Flexarr found the same titles in. Sonarr's /tv/Severance (2022) and Flexarr's /data/media/tv/Severance (2022) mean /tv is /data/media/tv. When enough titles agree, Flexarr saves the mapping itself, on its next library scan, and the line goes green. When it's less sure, the line is amber: Use this saves the folder Flexarr suggests. Choose another or Choose folder lets you pick the folder on the server yourself. The app's line under Apps also says when one of its folders isn't found. To write a mapping yourself, choose Edit by hand (or Add one by hand). In Path in the app, type the path the *arr app uses, such as /tv. In Path on this server, type where Flexarr sees the same folder, such as /data/media/tv. Then choose Save. Mappings apply straight away, and titles that weren't linked to Sonarr, Radarr or Lidarr are matched again. If you take out a mapping Flexarr saved itself, it doesn't add it back. #In config.json The same mappings are kept in the server's config.json (in /config in Docker, ~/.flexarr/data on a Mac) as pathMappings: { "pathMappings": [ { "from": "/tv", "to": "/data/media/tv" }, { "from": "/movies", "to": "/data/media/movies" } ] } from is the path in Sonarr, Radarr or Lidarr; to is the path Flexarr sees. Leave the rest of the file as it is. Flexarr notices the change by itself; restart it if it doesn't seem to. #How mappings are applied A mapping covers its folder and everything inside it: /tv maps /tv/Some Show/Season 1/episode.mkv to /data/media/tv/Some Show/Season 1/episode.mkv. It matches whole folder

title: Requests
description: Find films and shows you don't have yet in Discover, and request them through Seerr from the web app or the Apple TV.
text: With Seerr connected, Flexarr can show you films and shows you don't have yet, and request them in one go. Seerr passes the request to Radarr or Sonarr, they download it, and it turns up in your library. Seerr and Overseerr both work. #Before you start Connect Seerr in Settings › Connections: choose the pencil beside Seerr, type its Address (usually http://<host>:5055) and its API key (in Seerr, under Settings › General), and choose Save. See Connect Sonarr, Radarr, Lidarr and Seerr. Seerr itself needs Radarr and Sonarr set up in its own settings, since it hands requests to them. For requested titles to show up the moment they're downloaded, set up the webhooks too. Note Requests are for films and shows. Music isn't requested through Seerr. #Where you can request Where Discover Request Web app Yes Yes Apple TV Yes Yes iPhone and iPad Not yet Not yet On iPhone and iPad you'll still hear when something you asked for arrives (see Status). #On the web Choose Discover in the sidebar. With Seerr connected, it starts with rows from Seerr: Trending this week Popular films Popular shows Coming to cinemas Below them is Your library by genre, which is everything you already have. Each poster is marked if you already have it or it's already been asked for. For anything else, choose Request under the poster, or open it to see more about it first and choose Request there. #Search for anything The search box at the top of Discover, Search for any film or show, looks beyond your library. Type a title and you get every matching film and show, with the ones you already have marked. Request anything else from the results. #Missing films in a collection A film series collection lists the films you don't have under Not in your library, each with its own Request button. #On the Apple TV Discover is in the sidebar, above Search. It shows the same rows as the web: what's trending, popular films and shows, and what's coming to cinemas. Select a title you don't have to open it. You'll see its ratings, cast, who made it, and more like it. Select Request. Press Menu to go back to Discover. A title you already have is marked with a gold play badge on its poster, and opens as itself. Search, at the top of Discover next to Browse, finds any film or show, not only what's in your library, so you can request it from there. Without Seerr connected, Discover on the Apple TV shows your library by genre, and says where to connect Seerr. #Who can request Any profile can request, with one exception: a profile that can't see any of your film libraries can't request films, and one that can't see any TV libraries can't request shows. Libraries a profile sees are set in Settings › Profiles. Hidden libraries are left out of Discover and requests for that profile too. See Profiles. Flexarr sends every request to Seerr with its own API key. Seerr doesn't know which profile asked: it handles the request under the rules of the Seerr account that key belongs to, which decides whether it's approved automatically. Shows are requested with all their seasons. #Status and when it arrives A title's button changes to show where it stands: You see What it means Request Not in your library and not asked for. Requested Seerr has it. Radarr or Sonarr will download it when they find it. Partly in your library Some of it is here already, such as some seasons of a show. In your library You have it. Try again The request didn't go through, perhaps because it's already been requested. Flexarr remembers who asked for what. When the film or show arrives, whoever requested it gets a Your request is ready notification on their iPhone or iPad, if notifications are on for that profile. See Notifications and widgets. To follow a request while it downloads, use Seerr itself, or Coming soon in Flexarr's sidebar for what Sonarr and Radarr are expecting. #If requests don't work Discover has no Seerr rows: check Seerr shows a green dot in Settings › Connections.
