title: Playback and transcoding
description: How Flexarr plays a file as it is, repackages it, or converts it, and how to set up hardware acceleration on your server.
headings: Three ways a file can play
text: Every time you press Play, Flexarr works out the least it has to do for that screen to show the file. Most of the time that's nothing at all. This page explains the three ways a file can reach you, what your server needs for the hardest of them, and how to see which one is happening. #Three ways a file can play #Direct play: the file as it is When a device can open the file and decode its picture and sound, Flexarr sends the file untouched. The server does no more work than a file share would. This is the best case: full quality, and the lightest load on the server. On Apple TV, iPhone and iPad, Play files directly is on by default. With it, the app opens almost any file itself, including MKV and AVI files and AV1, VC-1, MPEG-2 and XviD video, decoding in software what the hardware can't. HDR and Dolby Vision stay as they are. The server only steps in for the few files the app can't open. #Repackaging: same picture, new wrapping Sometimes the picture is fine but the file around it isn't. A typical case is an MKV with H.264 or HEVC video, when Play files directly is off. Flexarr then copies the original picture into a stream the device accepts, cut at the file's own keyframes. Nothing is re-encoded, so you lose no quality, HDR and Dolby Vision included, and the server barely notices. Starting and seeking stay instant. MKV files can be repackaged straight away. Other files are indexed in the background the first time they're played, and repackage from the next time. #Transcoding: converting as it plays When the device can't decode the picture, or the stream has to be smaller, Flexarr converts the file as you watch, to H.264 video. It converts only what you're about to watch, so you can still jump anywhere in a film instantly. HDR is converted to SDR on the way. Converting is real work for the server. By default it converts at most three videos at once. Beyond that, the player says the server is busy rather than slowing everyone down. #Hardware acceleration Converting video on the server's graphics chip is much faster and lighter than on its processor. Choose how in Settings › Streaming › Hardware acceleration. This page belongs to the main profile, the one that manages the server. Choice For Automatic (recommended) Apple VideoToolbox on a Mac. Anywhere else, Automatic means the processor, so pick one of the options below. Apple VideoToolbox Macs. Automatic already picks this. VA-API (Intel and AMD on Linux) Intel and AMD graphics on Linux. A VA-API device field appears, set to /dev/dri/renderD128 unless you change it. Intel Quick Sync Intel processors with built-in graphics. NVIDIA NVENC NVIDIA graphics cards. Off: convert on the CPU No graphics chip, or for troubleshooting. A Software speed choice appears. Only the options your server's copy of FFmpeg was built with are listed. Being listed doesn't prove the hardware is reachable, though. In Docker, for example, the container also needs the graphics device passed through to it. After changing this, play something that needs converting and check it starts (see How to tell what's happening, below). Note On a Mac, files whose video the graphics chip can't decode (old AVI and XviD files, VC-1) are decoded on the processor and still encoded on the graphics chip. You don't need to do anything. #Without a graphics chip With Off: convert on the CPU, Software speed offers Fastest, lowest quality, Fast (recommended) and Slower, better quality. Faster uses less of the server, at some cost to picture quality. Converting video in software is demanding. A recent multi-core desktop processor can usually keep up with a 1080p stream or two. A low-power NAS processor may struggle with even one, and converting 4K or HDR in software is heavy for almost anything. If your server has no graphics chip, the good news is that Apple devices rarely need converting at all, thanks to Play files directly and repackaging. #Limiting quality Settings › Streaming › Limit each stream to caps every stream from the

title: HDR and Dolby Atmos
description: How Flexarr gets HDR10, HLG, Dolby Vision, Atmos and lossless surround to your Apple TV, and the Apple TV settings that matter.
headings: Set up the Apple TV first
text: If you have a 4K HDR television and a soundbar or receiver, you want the picture and sound to arrive as they are in the file. Flexarr is built to do that on Apple TV, without converting anything. This page explains what reaches your TV, and the few settings on the Apple TV itself that make the difference. Note The Apple TV app isn't on the App Store yet. Until it is, you can install it from Xcode. #Set up the Apple TV first These are Apple's own settings, in the Apple TV's Settings › Video and Audio. They matter more than anything in Flexarr. Format: set it to the best your television supports. Apple recommends 4K SDR (or 4K SDR 60Hz) when you turn on matching below, so menus look right and HDR switches on only for HDR films. Match Content › Match Dynamic Range: turn this on. The Apple TV then switches the television into HDR10, HLG or Dolby Vision to suit each film, and back again afterwards. Match Content › Match Frame Rate: turn this on too. Films shot at 24 frames a second then play at 24, without judder. Audio Format: leave this on its automatic setting so the Apple TV sends Dolby Atmos to equipment that takes it. If Atmos isn't showing on your soundbar or receiver, check here that Dolby Atmos is available. Flexarr follows Match Content: when it's on, the Apple TV switches mode for each title Flexarr plays. Tip Without Match Dynamic Range, an Apple TV set to a fixed Dolby Vision output has no HDR10 mode. A plain HDR10 film may then be converted to SDR when it reaches the Apple TV as a stream from the server. Turning on Match Dynamic Range avoids this. #HDR: what reaches your TV With Play files directly on (the default on Apple TV, iPhone and iPad), the Apple TV plays the file itself. HDR10, HLG and Dolby Vision reach the television untouched. With Play files directly off, the server repackages the original picture into a stream without re-encoding it. Here's what the television gets: In the file On the television HDR10 HDR10, as it is HLG HLG, as it is Dolby Vision profile 5 Dolby Vision, on a Dolby Vision television Dolby Vision profile 8.1 Dolby Vision on a Dolby Vision television, otherwise HDR10 Dolby Vision profile 7 (UHD Blu-ray) Its HDR10 base layer HDR10+ HDR10, with its HDR10+ scene-by-scene metadata kept for televisions that use it A film's details say HDR10+ when its file carries HDR10+, and Dolby Vision, HDR10+ when it has both. HDR is only converted to SDR when it has to be: when the television doesn't show HDR, when the stream is limited in size (see Limit each stream to in Playback and transcoding), or when the video itself has to be converted. On iPhone and iPad, HDR shows on screens that support it. #Sound: Atmos, TrueHD and DTS How the sound reaches your equipment depends on what's in the file. #Dolby Atmos in Dolby Digital Plus This is the kind of Atmos you'll find on most streaming-service releases. It reaches the Apple TV intact and signalled as Atmos, ready for an Atmos receiver, soundbar or HomePods. #TrueHD, DTS-HD Master Audio and PCM The Apple TV can't play these as they are, so Flexarr makes sure nothing is lost on the way. Play files directly on, Lossless surround on: the app decodes the soundtrack and sends it as multichannel PCM over HDMI. Use this with a receiver or an eARC soundbar that accepts it. Play files directly on, Lossless surround off: they're sent as Dolby Digital Plus, which any soundbar or receiver plays. Play files directly off: the server sends them as lossless FLAC, up to 7.1, instead of squeezing them into 5.1. Plain DTS is decoded with nothing more lost on the way. Note TrueHD soundtracks with Atmos currently play as lossless surround without Atmos's height channels. Keeping them is on the roadmap. #Turning on Lossless surround On the Apple TV, open Flexarr's Settings › Playback. Under This Apple TV, turn on Play files directly if it's off, then Lossless surround. The same switches are in the iPhone and iPad app's Settings › Playback, for AirPlay or a connected display. Lea

title: Subtitles, skipping and Up Next
description: Subtitles of every kind, skipping intros, recaps and credits, the next-episode countdown and scrubbing previews.
text: Flexarr's own player on Apple TV, iPhone and iPad, and the web player, share the same features for subtitles and getting through a series. Your choices belong to your profile, so they follow you from the TV to your phone. #Subtitles #What Flexarr finds Flexarr picks up these kinds of subtitles: Embedded: tracks inside the video file, as most MKV files have. Closed captions carried inside the video itself, as American TV recordings have them. They're listed as CC. Flexarr checks for them when it scans a file. Sidecar files: .srt, .vtt, .ass or .ssa files beside the video, named after it. Add a language and, if you like, forced or sdh before the extension: Heat (1995).mkv Heat (1995).en.srt Heat (1995).en.sdh.srt Heat (1995).en.forced.srt Sonarr, Radarr and most subtitle tools name files this way already. Subtitles come as text (SRT, WebVTT, ASS and the like) or pictures (PGS from Blu-rays, VobSub from DVDs, DVB from broadcasts). Text subtitles are drawn by the player at the size you choose. Picture subtitles are drawn by the app on Apple TV, iPhone and iPad when Play files directly is on. In a web browser they have to be burned into the picture, which means the server converts the video while they're on. #Styled subtitles ASS and SSA subtitles, as most anime has, can carry their own fonts, colours, positions, signs and karaoke. The web player draws them exactly as they were made, with the fonts attached to the file. On Apple TV, iPhone and iPad they keep their colours and go where they were placed, such as a sign at the top of the picture, in your caption style's font. #Closed captions and teletext Closed captions carried inside the video, as American TV recordings have them, are listed as CC and work on every device. Flexarr looks for them when it scans a file. Teletext subtitles, as European TV recordings carry them, show on Apple TV, iPhone and iPad with Play files directly on. The subtitles menu there has a Teletext page choice for channels that don't use the usual page, such as 888 in the UK or 150 and 777 in Germany. On Android and in a web browser, teletext shows only when the server's FFmpeg can read it, as the Docker image's can; a server on a Mac can't. Android's subtitles menu has the same Teletext page choice. #Finding subtitles When a film or episode has no subtitles in your language, or the ones it has are out of time, Flexarr can fetch some through Bazarr. It works for what Sonarr and Radarr manage, in the languages Bazarr is set up for, and every profile can use it. In the player, open the subtitles menu and choose Search for subtitles…. On a title's page in the web app, it's under ⋯. Wait while Bazarr asks its subtitle sites. It can take a minute. Choose one and Download, or Pick the best for me. Those marked Matches your file were made for your exact copy, so they should be in time. The subtitles are saved beside the video, so every app sees them. In the player, the title carries on where it was with them on. Note Bazarr only searches for a film or show that has a languages profile. If it has none, the first search from Flexarr gives it Bazarr's first profile; for an episode, that's the whole show. From then on Bazarr looks after it like anything else with a profile, so if Bazarr is set to search for missing subtitles on a schedule, it will fetch them for that title by itself. To keep Bazarr to what you ask for, go to Settings › Scheduler in Bazarr and set Search for Missing Series Subtitles and Search for Missing Movies Subtitles to Never. If subtitles beside the video drift out of time, choose them, then Re-sync to audio. Bazarr lines them up with the soundtrack, which takes a minute or so, and the player picks up the new timing when it's done. For an offset that's the same all the way through, Timing in the subtitles menu is quicker. #Turning them on and off Choose a subtitle track, or Off, from the subtitles menu in the player. Flexarr remembers your choice for that film or show, so the next episode and th

title: Music
description: Music libraries with Lidarr's artwork and details, a queue, playlists, lyrics, daily mixes, artist radio and offline albums.
text: Flexarr plays your music library like a streaming app: artists with their pictures, albums on shelves, a queue, playlists and lyrics. It's at its fullest in the web app, with the Apple apps covering everyday listening. #Setting up a music library In Settings › Libraries, choose Add library, pick Music and point it at your music folder. If you use Lidarr, connect it in Settings › Connections. See Connect your *arrs. Lidarr isn't required, but it makes a big difference. With it, artists and albums take their names, years, descriptions and artwork from Lidarr: the artist's own picture rather than an album cover, and a cover for every album even when the files carry none. An artist's page shelves releases into Albums, EPs and singles, Live and compilations and Other. Without Lidarr, Flexarr reads everything from the files' tags. A track by someone other than the album's artist, such as a duet or a compilation track, shows its own artist. Compilations without an album artist are filed under Various Artists. #Playing and the queue Every artist, album and playlist has Play and Shuffle. An artist's Play runs through their whole catalogue, oldest album first. On the web, the now-playing bar stays with you as you browse. Tracks and albums have Play next and Add to queue in their menus. The queue panel above the bar lets you drag tracks into order, remove them, clear the lot or skip to any track. The queue and your place in it survive a page reload. On Apple TV, iPhone and iPad, the player has next and previous, seeking, shuffle and repeat, and shows the whole queue. Music carries on while you browse, and playing a film pauses it until you're done. #Now Playing on Apple TV While music plays, a Now Playing entry appears in the sidebar, with the cover, controls and the queue. Play/pause on the remote works from anywhere in the app. #On iPhone and iPad A mini-player sits above the tab bar. Tap it for the full Now Playing sheet, with the cover, scrubber, controls, queue and AirPlay. The lock screen, Control Center and a paired Apple Watch control playback too. #Playlists Each profile has its own playlists. On the web, choose Add to playlist from a track's, album's or artist's menu, and manage them from the Playlists page: rename, reorder by dragging, or delete. Playlists play on Apple TV, iPhone and iPad as well, and appear in a Your playlists row on Home. Making and editing playlists is on the web for now. #Lyrics Flexarr shows lyrics on the web, Apple TV, iPhone and iPad. On the web, they're in a Lyrics panel under the album's track list. In the apps, there's a Lyrics button on Now Playing. Timed lyrics follow the song with the current line lit, and choosing a line jumps there. Flexarr doesn't fetch lyrics from the internet. It reads them from your files, in this order: An .lrc file beside the track, with the same name (timed lyrics). Lyrics stored in the track's own tags. A .txt file beside the track, with the same name. Brothers in Arms/01 - So Far Away.flac Brothers in Arms/01 - So Far Away.lrc Any tool that saves .lrc files next to your music works. #Made for you, and radio These are on the web for now. Daily mixes: up to four for each profile, built from what it plays, grouping artists who share genres ("Rock Mix"). About 40 tracks each, the same all day and fresh tomorrow. They appear once a profile has played twenty or so tracks, in a Made for you row on Home and in a music library's Browse view. Artist radio: start it from an artist's page. It's a station of about fifty tracks from that artist and others sharing their genres. Home rows: Recently played, Most played, More from artists you play and New albums. Move them or turn them off in Settings › Home and Browse. #Gapless, crossfade and volume The web player loads the next track before the current one ends, so the switch between them takes a few milliseconds. Live albums and DJ mixes flow on almost without a gap. In the web app, Settings › Playback › Music in this browser has two

title: Podcasts
description: Follow podcasts from Apple's directory or any feed, with Up Next, speeds, a sleep timer, offline episodes on iPhone and iPad, and OPML import.
text: Podcasts are built into Flexarr. There's no library to add and nothing to set up: they sit with your libraries, and each profile follows its own shows. They're on the web, iPhone and iPad. They aren't on the Apple TV. #Finding shows Open Podcasts and choose Browse. Top charts, by category, come from Apple's podcast directory. Search finds any show in that directory. A feed's address works too: paste it into the search box to add a show Apple doesn't list, such as a private or members-only feed. Whose charts you see is set by the main profile in Settings › Libraries, under Podcasts › Charts and search. It starts as the server's own region. #Following a show Choose Follow on a show. It joins the row of shows you follow on the Podcasts page, and its newest episodes you haven't heard appear there and in a New podcasts row on Home. Flexarr checks feeds by itself, more often for shows that publish often. On a show's page: Unplayed episodes come first. Newest first or Oldest first sets the order. Oldest first suits shows heard in order, and Play then starts the oldest you haven't heard. A show you follow remembers its order. Mark all as played clears a back catalogue in one go. #Listening Episodes play in the same bar as music, and pick up where you left off on any device. 15 seconds back and 30 on, on screen and on the lock screen. Speeds from 0.8× to 3×. Your profile's default is in Settings › Podcasts › Speed, and changing it in the player changes it there too. Sleep timer: stop after a set time, or at the end of the episode. When an episode ends, the show's next one plays, or else the newest you haven't heard. Episodes play through your server rather than straight from the podcast's host. That means they work away from home over Tailscale as they do at home, and podcast hosts don't see where each listener is. #Up Next Up Next is your own queue of episodes, shared between the web and your phone. Use Play next or Add to Up Next on any episode. Reorder or remove episodes on the Podcasts page, or in Now Playing on iPhone and iPad. An episode leaves Up Next once it starts playing. #Settings Podcast settings belong to each profile. On the web, Settings › Podcasts: Show in the sidebar: either way, Home has a New podcasts row. Speed. Download new episodes and Episodes to keep, for iPhone and iPad. On iPhone and iPad, Settings › Podcasts has Auto-download new episodes, how many of the newest to keep, and Speed. #Offline on iPhone and iPad Download any episode to listen with no connection. Or turn on Auto-download new episodes: the newest unplayed episodes of every show you follow then download by themselves, and played ones are cleared away. Episodes you deleted yourself are never downloaded again by themselves. Automatic downloads wait for Wi-Fi, unless you turn off Automatic downloads on Wi-Fi only in Settings › Downloads. They never use Low Data Mode. An episode you download by hand comes over mobile data too. What you hear offline counts once you're back online. #The episodes folder on the server To reach your phone, an episode is first fetched to your server, then the phone takes it and the server deletes its copy. It waits in the Podcasts Episodes folder, in Settings › Libraries. This starts as a folder in Flexarr's own data folder. If that's on a small drive, choose Change and pick a folder on your media drive instead. #Bringing your shows over Most podcast apps can export the shows you follow as an OPML file. In Flexarr on the web, use Import on the Podcasts page and choose that file. Export gives you an OPML file of your shows to take elsewhere. #Notifications and widgets On iPhone and iPad, Flexarr can tell you when a show you follow has a new episode, with buttons to play or download it. Turn this on in Settings › Notifications. There are widgets for Continue listening and Up Next too. See Notifications and widgets. #Siri Siri plays podcasts on iPhone and iPad: "Play The Rest Is History in Flexarr" plays the episode you'd hear

title: Watchlist
description: Keep a list of films and shows to watch later, whether you have them yet or not, and hear when they arrive.
text: Each profile has its own watchlist: films and shows you want to watch later, whether they're in your library yet or not. When something on it arrives, you hear about it, and it waits on Home under Ready from your watchlist. #Adding and removing Where How Web app Watchlist on a title's page, the bookmark under a poster in Discover and search, or Add to watchlist in a poster's menu. iPhone and iPad Watchlist on a film's or show's page, Add to watchlist when you press and hold a poster, or tap a title under Not in your library in Search. Apple TV Watchlist on a title's page (Discover's too), or Add to watchlist when you press and hold a poster. Android Watchlist on a film's or show's page, Add to watchlist when you press and hold a poster, or tap a title under Not in your library in Search. Siri "Save Severance in Flexarr" for a title in your library, or "Add to my watchlist in Flexarr" and then say any title, whether you have it yet or not. Assistants Ask an assistant connected over MCP to add or remove a title, even one you don't have yet. Choose On watchlist on its page to take a title off again, or Remove from watchlist when you press and hold its poster (on the web, the bookmark on its card). Adding a title twice keeps one, and adding one you took off brings it back. Titles leave the list by themselves once you've dealt with them: a film when you've watched it, a show when you've started it (it carries on in Continue watching). A title you've seen before stays until you watch it again. #Your watchlist On the web, Watchlist is in the sidebar under Browse. On iPhone, iPad and Android it's at the top of Libraries, and on the Apple TV it's in the sidebar beside Discover. Android and iPhone have a Watchlist widget too (see Notifications and widgets). Each title says where it's got to: You see What it means Its usual poster It's in your library. Play it. On its way It's been requested, or Sonarr or Radarr are getting it. Out and a date It isn't released yet. Request It's out, but nobody's asked for it. Choose Request to add it to your library (see Requests). A title you don't have also says which streaming services it's on, such as On Netflix, for the country set as Streaming Region in Seerr. Every app can show only one kind (Ready to watch, On its way, Coming or Not available), only films or only shows, and sort the list: Ready first (the default), Recently added, Release date (newest first) or Title. Titles you don't have yet need Seerr connected (see Requests). Without it, you can still keep a watchlist of what's in your library. #When something arrives When a title on your watchlist arrives in your library, your iPhone, iPad or Android phone says From your watchlist, if that profile has notifications on. It follows the Requests switch in the app's notification settings. If you also requested the title, you hear once, as Your request is ready. See Notifications and widgets. #Requesting what you add The main profile can have a profile's watchlist request what it adds: open Settings › Profiles, edit the profile, and turn on Request what … adds to the watchlist. It's off to start with, and only shows when Seerr is connected. With it on, a film or show that isn't in your library and hasn't been asked for is requested as soon as it's added. It never requests: titles that are already in your library or already requested films for a profile that can't see any film library, or shows for one that can't see any TV library titles brought across from another service rather than added in Flexarr Taking a title off the watchlist doesn't cancel its request.

title: Trakt
description: Keep what you watch, where you're up to and your watchlist in step with Trakt, both ways.
text: Connect a profile to your Trakt account and Flexarr keeps the two in step: what you watch, where you're up to, and your watchlist. Each profile connects its own account, and nothing is shared until that person connects. #Connecting Open Settings › Trakt in the web app, on iPhone, iPad or Android, or on the Apple TV or Android TV. Choose Connect. Flexarr shows a code. On any phone or computer, go to trakt.tv/activate and enter the code. On a TV, scan the QR code to open that page on your phone. On iPhone and Android, Copy code and open Trakt copies the code and opens the page; on the web, Copy code. You don't need to wait on that screen: your server waits for the code for 10 minutes. Once you've entered it, Settings › Trakt shows your Trakt name. A Trakt account can be connected to one profile only, so nothing is counted twice. #Bringing your history across Once you're connected, Bring your Trakt history across shows you what would change before anything does (See what changes on the web). For example: Trakt has 12 films and 340 episodes. 200 are here, 41 not yet watched in Flexarr. Choose Bring across to go ahead. Anything watched on Trakt is marked watched in Flexarr, with the date you watched it. Anything watched in Flexarr that Trakt doesn't have goes to Trakt. Titles you've watched that aren't on your server yet are remembered. When one arrives, it's already marked watched. Nothing is ever marked unwatched, on either side. It's offered once. When it's done, Settings says History brought across; after that, everything stays in step by itself. To bring it across again, disconnect and connect again. #Staying in step After that, it all happens by itself: What How Watching Trakt shows what you're watching while it plays. When Flexarr counts a film or episode as watched (near the end, or once the end credits start), so does Trakt. Marking watched Mark as watched in Flexarr goes to Trakt, and so does anything you watched on a download away from the server. Watched elsewhere Plays in other apps connected to Trakt come to Flexarr within a few minutes. Where you're up to Stop part way and Trakt keeps your place. Stop in another app connected to Trakt, and Flexarr picks up from there. Your watchlist Add or remove a title in either place, and it's added or removed in the other. Titles that come from Trakt are never requested by themselves; they show Request if they're not here. Marking something unwatched in Flexarr leaves Trakt as it is: your Trakt history stays true, and Flexarr won't mark it watched again. Sync now in Settings › Trakt checks straight away rather than waiting (once a minute at most). Everything a connected profile watches goes to Trakt, whichever library it's in, and Trakt profiles are public unless you make yours private on trakt.tv. #Lists and picks Lists: in Settings › Trakt, choose any of your Trakt lists, or ones you've liked, and each shows up in Collections on the web, just for you, kept in step with Trakt. Titles on the list that are here show as usual. Films that aren't here show with Request. For you, from Trakt: once you're connected, Discover on the web, Apple TV and Android TV has a row of Trakt's picks for you, with titles you have first and ones you've watched left out. #If something's wrong You see What to do Trakt signed Flexarr out You revoked Flexarr on trakt.tv, or it wasn't used for months. Choose Connect again; your history stays. Trakt's watchlist is full A free Trakt account holds a limited number of titles. New titles stay on Flexarr's watchlist; make room on Trakt and they'll go across. Waiting to send Trakt or your internet is down. Flexarr keeps the changes and sends them when it can. No Trakt in Settings Kids profiles don't have Trakt. Otherwise, your server can't reach Flexarr's Trakt service. Check it can reach the internet. Disconnect in Settings › Trakt stops it all and makes Trakt forget Flexarr. What you've watched stays as it is, in both places. Making a profile a kids profile, or

title: Downloads
description: Keep films, episodes, albums, playlists and podcasts on your iPhone or iPad to watch and listen with no connection.
text: The iPhone and iPad app can keep films, episodes, albums, playlists and podcast episodes on the device, for a flight, a train or anywhere without a signal. Downloads are on iPhone and iPad only. #Downloading something Tap the download button on a film's or episode's page, on an album or playlist, or on a podcast episode. It starts straight away. The button shows how it's going: An hourglass, "Getting ready": your server is preparing it. Wi-Fi: it's waiting for Wi-Fi. A filling ring: it's coming down to the device. A green tick: it's ready to play with no connection. An exclamation mark: it failed. Tap it to see why, and to Try again. Tap the button while a download is under way to stop or remove it. Downloads carry on with the app closed, and pick up where they left off if interrupted. Everything you've downloaded is in the Downloads tab, where it plays with Skip Intro and the countdown to the next episode as usual. #What your server does first Your server gets each download ready before it's sent, one at a time. It converts a film or episode to a size and format the phone plays, or sends it as it is when it can. It does this quietly in the background and waits while anyone is watching something that's being converted, so a download never slows someone's film down. A prepared download that isn't collected within a week is deleted from the server. #Picture size Choose the size once, in the app's Settings › Downloads › Size: Automatic (720p): the default. Looks good on a phone and doesn't take much space. Sound is stereo. Original: the full picture and sound, but takes the most space. A title whose original won't play on the phone comes at 1080p instead. Small (480p): the least space, for a long trip on a small phone. Text subtitles come with the download. Picture-based subtitles (from Blu-rays and DVDs) don't. Albums, playlists and podcasts come as their files are when the phone can play them: AAC, ALAC, MP3, FLAC, WAV and AIFF. Anything else is converted to AAC. #Automatic downloads In Settings › Downloads: Download the next episode: on by default. Once you've downloaded an episode, the next one downloads too. Episodes are deleted a day after you finish them. Automatic downloads on Wi-Fi only: on by default. Downloads the app starts by itself, like the next episode or new podcast episodes, wait for Wi-Fi. Turn this off to let them use mobile data too. Automatic downloads never use Low Data Mode. Downloads you start yourself use mobile data as well as Wi-Fi. For podcasts, Auto-download new episodes in Settings › Podcasts keeps the newest unplayed episodes of every show you follow on the device. See Podcasts. #Storage Settings › Downloads shows the space your downloads use, under Storage, and has Delete all downloads. To remove one thing, tap its download button and remove it. A podcast episode you delete is never downloaded again by itself. Signing out of the server on the device deletes its downloads. #Watch progress What you watch and hear offline is sent to your server when the device is back online. Resume points, watched ticks and Continue Watching then catch up on every other screen. #Two devices on one profile An iPhone and an iPad on the same profile each get their own copy of a download. New podcast episodes download by themselves on both. #Downloading away from home Downloads work away from home over Tailscale as well as at home. A big Original download over a slow home upload can take a while, so it's best started at home on Wi-Fi.

title: Your iPhone as a remote
description: Control what's playing on your Apple TV from your iPhone or iPad: pause, scrub, skip the intro, change subtitles and sound, pick another episode, and carry on watching on the phone.
text: When an Apple TV in your home is playing something from Flexarr, the iPhone and iPad apps show a Playing on TV bar above the tabs. It shows the TVs playing for the profile chosen on the phone, so each person sees their own: Claire's film on the bedroom TV doesn't show on Dan's phone. There's nothing to set up: the TV and the phone only need to be signed in to the same server, with the TV's Flexarr app open. The bar has play/pause. Tap it for the remote. The × hides the bar until that TV plays a different show or film; it doesn't stop anything, so it's safe while someone else is watching. #The remote Scrubber: drag to anywhere in the film or episode. Underneath is how far in it is, how long is left and when it ends. Back and forward 10 seconds, and previous and next episode. Previous starts the episode again, or goes to the one before if you're near the start. Skip Intro, Skip Recap and Next Episode appear here whenever the TV shows them. Audio and subtitles, speed and sound (dialogue boost, night mode and speakers): each is lit while it's set to something other than normal. Continue on iPhone stops the film or episode on the TV and carries on from the same moment on your phone. The TV goes back to the title's page and says Now playing on iPhone. Stop stops it on the TV. For a few seconds you can Undo, which starts it again from where it stopped. Episodes lists the season: tap one to play it on the TV. A title from a library hidden from your profile shows as playing but not what it is. You can pause, skip and stop it, but not continue it on your phone, undo a stop, or change its tracks or sound. With more than one TV playing, tap the TV's name at the top to switch between them. For the TV's menus and its volume, use the Remote in Control Center, as before. If a button doesn't work (the TV has gone to sleep, or its Flexarr app is closed), the phone says why. Note A few buttons need the TV's Flexarr app to be up to date, and the phone only shows the ones it can do. If the phone is signed in with the server's key rather than as its own device, the bar can take up to half a minute to catch up with changes made on the TV. #On the Lock Screen While the remote is following a TV, your phone shows what's playing on the Lock Screen and in the Dynamic Island, with back 10 seconds, play/pause and forward 10. Tap it to open the remote. It keeps up while the phone is locked, as long as notifications are on for your server. To keep the title private, your phone puts the title and picture there itself. Only whether it's paused, how far in it is, how long it is and its speed travel through Flexarr's notification service, because Apple reads these updates directly and they can't be encrypted like notifications. Anyone holding your locked phone can pause or skip the TV from it, as with any Lock Screen controls. To turn it off, go to Settings › Flexarr › Live Activities on the phone. Swiping it away hides it for that title.

title: Live TV and recording
description: Watch TV channels in Flexarr with a guide, favourites and rewind, and record programmes and series, using Dispatcharr as the source.
text: Flexarr can show TV channels next to your films and shows, with a programme guide, favourites, pause and rewind, and recording. It doesn't come with any channels. You bring your own, through Dispatcharr. Live TV is on the web, Apple TV, iPhone and iPad. #What you need Flexarr reads channels and their guide from Dispatcharr, a free, self-hosted app that gathers TV sources into one channel list. Dispatcharr is the only source Flexarr supports. You can't give Flexarr an M3U playlist or XMLTV guide address directly; add them to Dispatcharr instead. Into Dispatcharr you can bring: Your own tuner, such as an HDHomeRun on an aerial or cable connection, for free-to-air channels. An IPTV service you're entitled to use, given to Dispatcharr as an M3U playlist with an XMLTV guide. Setting up Dispatcharr itself is covered in its own documentation. Once it has channels and a guide, carry on below. Important Only use sources you have the right to watch. Flexarr doesn't provide, find or recommend channels. #Connecting Dispatcharr First, in Dispatcharr: Add a user for Flexarr, at Streamer level. Give it a long, random XC password. This works as Flexarr's key. It can only list and play channels, never sign in to Dispatcharr or change anything. Give that user the channels you want in Flexarr. Then in Flexarr, as the main profile: Open Settings › Connections and edit Dispatcharr. Fill in Address (for example http://localhost:9191), User name and Key (XC password). Choose Test. It should say how many channels it found and how many connections your source allows at a time. Then choose Save. The channels and guide come in straight away. The guide refreshes every six hours, and channels you add or remove in Dispatcharr show up within five minutes. Refresh channels and guide fetches them now. Channel logos come from a community logo collection where it has a match, and from Dispatcharr where it doesn't. #Watching Live TV sits with your libraries. On the web, On now lists every channel with what's on, how far through it is and what's next, filtered by group. The Guide shows the next six hours, or up to a day, as a grid. On Apple TV, the guide has categories down the left and channels with three hours across. What's on now plays; anything later shows what it is. On iPhone and iPad, Live TV is a list of channels. The Guide button turns it into a grid, and List goes back. In the player, previous and next change channel. The Channels button lists every channel over the picture, with Last watched at the top so flipping between two is one press. On Apple TV, the Guide button opens the guide over the picture while the channel carries on behind it. Home has a Live TV row too, starting with the channel you watched last, then your favourites. #Favourites Star the channels you watch most. Each profile has its own, and Live TV opens on them. Web: select the star on a channel. Apple TV: press and hold a channel or programme. iPhone and iPad: swipe right on a channel, or press and hold. #Pause and rewind You can pause a channel and rewind it. The timeline shows the time of day, LIVE or how far behind you are, and a button to jump back to live. The server keeps the rewind window while anyone is watching a channel, so you can rewind to when the channel was first put on, up to the limit. Set the limit in Settings › Live TV › Rewind up to, from 15 minutes to 4 hours (1 hour to start with). It takes about 2 GB of space an hour for HD. #Picture and sound Channels that are already H.264 play as they come. Others (interlaced, MPEG-2 and HEVC) are converted, and interlaced channels are made smooth at 50 frames a second. On Apple TV, iPhone and iPad at home, channels broadcasting Dolby Digital or Dolby Digital Plus come through as 5.1. The web player is stereo. One channel is shared by everyone watching it, so a source that allows one connection can still serve the whole house. #Watching away from home Away from home, over Tailscale or the internet, channels come in a reduce

title: Profiles
description: Give everyone in the house their own Continue Watching, history and settings, with an optional PIN, and choose which libraries each profile sees.
headings: What each profile keeps to itself
Choosing which libraries a profile sees
text: A profile is one person's view of Flexarr. Everyone in the household can have their own, so your half-watched film doesn't turn up in someone else's Continue Watching, and their cartoons don't fill your "Because you watched" row. #What each profile keeps to itself Each profile has its own: Continue Watching, watched history and Up Next Playback settings: auto-play the next episode, skip intros, recaps and credits, and subtitle size. These follow the profile to every device, the Apple TV included. Podcasts: the shows it follows, its Up Next queue and its podcast settings Music: playlists, daily mixes, and recently and most played Collections of its own (the main profile can also make collections for the whole household) Live TV favourites and the channel it watched last Libraries: which ones it can see at all (see below) A picture, a name and a colour Things that belong to the server, such as your libraries, connections to Sonarr, Radarr and Lidarr, and the layout of Home, are the same for everyone. #The main profile The first profile, made when you set Flexarr up, is the main profile. It manages the server, and it has a crown beside its name in Settings › Profiles and on its picture when you choose who's watching. Only the main profile can: change the server's settings, libraries and connections add, edit and remove profiles connect new devices, and see or replace the API key fix a wrong match, or delete a title through Sonarr or Radarr make and change the household's collections allow or block a title for kids, analyse a title, or scan a library for changes Every other profile can browse, watch, listen, make requests through Seerr, and open Settings to change its own playback and podcast settings. #Unlocking settings Flexarr has an admin PIN: you choose it when you set Flexarr up. It belongs to the server, apart from the main profile's own PIN (see PINs). Watching as the main profile doesn't need it, and nor does tidying the library from a title's or library's page (the last three things above). Changing the server's settings, profiles and devices does. Open Settings on the main profile and the server's pages say Settings are locked: enter the admin PIN and choose Unlock. Settings stay unlocked on that browser or device for 15 minutes after your last change. They lock again sooner if someone else is chosen there, if you choose Lock settings at the bottom of the list, or if the server restarts. Being on your home network doesn't skip the admin PIN. A device asking to connect still shows up on the main profile while settings are locked. Choosing Allow asks for the admin PIN first. If there's no admin PIN yet (a server set up before Flexarr asked for one), Settings asks you to choose one before anything else. To keep the main profile's watch history private, give it a PIN of its own in Settings › Profiles, as for anyone. Choosing it then asks for that PIN; the admin PIN works there too. #Adding a profile On the web, signed in as the main profile: Go to Settings › Profiles and choose Add a profile. Give it a name, and if you like a picture and a colour. Choose Add a PIN if it should be private. Untick any libraries it shouldn't see. Choose Add profile. If you bring your history over from Plex, your Plex Home profile pictures can come too. See Import from Plex. #PINs A PIN is 4 to 8 digits. Without one, anyone can switch to that profile. With one, Flexarr asks for it whenever someone chooses the profile. The main profile's PIN works like anyone's: add it, change it or remove it in Settings › Profiles. It can be the same as the admin PIN or different. The admin PIN is in Settings › Security. It can be changed but not removed, and changing it takes the current one. If you've forgotten it, see I forgot a profile's PIN. Without a PIN of its own, the main profile is chosen freely on browsers and devices you signed in. title: Watch away from home
description: Reach your Flexarr server from anywhere with Tailscale, with no ports opened on your router, or through an HTTPS reverse proxy.
text: At home, your devices find Flexarr on the Wi-Fi. Away from home, they need a safe way back to it. The easiest is Tailscale, and it's the one Flexarr is built around. If you already run an HTTPS reverse proxy, that works too. #Tailscale Tailscale is a free app that puts your devices on a small private network of their own, called a tailnet. Your phone can then reach your server from a hotel or a train as if it were at home. The connection is encrypted, and nothing is opened on your router, so Flexarr isn't on the public internet. #Set it up On the server, install Tailscale from tailscale.com/download and sign in. In Flexarr on the web, signed in as the main profile, go to Settings › Access. Under Away from home, Tailscale should say it's connected. Choose Turn on. Flexarr shows its Private address, something like https://your-server.your-tailnet.ts.net:8443. It's HTTPS, with a real certificate from Tailscale. On your iPhone or iPad, install Tailscale from the App Store and sign in with the same account. Leave it connected. Open the Flexarr app once while you're at home, so it learns the private address. From then on, the iPhone, iPad and Apple TV apps switch by themselves. When the home address doesn't answer, they use the Tailscale one, and they go back to the home address when you're home again. There's nothing to change in the apps. In a browser away from home, open the private address instead of the usual one. Note Flexarr needs the tailscale command on the same computer it runs on to turn this on. In Docker it can't see the Tailscale installed around it, so Settings › Access says Not available in Docker. To use Flexarr away from home from Docker, put it behind an HTTPS reverse proxy, or run Flexarr without Docker on a computer with Tailscale. #Who can get in When you first turn it on, your own Tailscale account is linked to the main profile. Anyone else you invite to your tailnet appears under People on your tailnet in Settings › Access. Choose a profile for each person. Anyone set to Not allowed is turned away, even though Tailscale lets them reach the server. Over Tailscale, watching works as it does at home. Changing settings is stricter: you'll be asked to choose the main profile with the admin PIN. That browser then stays signed in until it's signed out, or left unused for two weeks. See Unlocking settings for the admin PIN. Important Someone on your tailnet whose account is linked to another profile can only choose the main profile with the admin PIN, even if it has a PIN of its own. Changing settings over Tailscale asks for the admin PIN, as it does at home. Don't use Tailscale Funnel for Flexarr. Funnel publishes an address to the whole internet. If Flexarr spots it, Settings warns you; turn remote access off and on again to make it private. #Quality away from home Hotel Wi-Fi and phone data are slower than your home network, and so is the upload speed of most home broadband. Live TV comes in a reduced version away from home: at most 720p, at about 2.5 Mbps, in stereo. At home, channels play as they come. Films and shows play as they do at home unless you set a limit. In Settings › Streaming, Limit each stream to caps every stream; 4 Mbps is a good choice for watching away. The limit applies at home too. On the web, the player's quality menu lets you choose 1080p, 720p or 480p for one viewing. On iPhone and iPad, downloading before you leave avoids the question altogether. See Downloads. #An HTTPS reverse proxy instead If you already run a reverse proxy such as nginx, Caddy or Traefik with an HTTPS certificate, you can put Flexarr behind it. If the proxy runs on another computer, or in Docker, tell Flexarr to believe the visitor addresses it passes on. Add it to trustedProxies in config.json, in the server's data folder, as a list of addresses or ranges: { "trustedProxies": ["172.17.0.1", "10.0.0.0/24"] } Without it, everyone who comes through that proxy counts as the internet and has to sign in. title: Siri and Shortcuts
description: Ask Siri on your iPhone or iPad to play a film, the next episode of a show or a podcast, here or on your Apple TV, and build your own shortcuts.
text: Once the Flexarr app on your iPhone or iPad has signed in to your server, Siri understands it. There's nothing to set up. Siri learns the titles in your library when the app signs in, so it knows what you mean by "The Traitors" or "Heat". Every phrase needs the word Flexarr in it, so Siri knows which app you mean. #Things to say #Films and shows "Play the next episode of Curb Your Enthusiasm in Flexarr" "Play Heat in Flexarr" or "Watch Heat in Flexarr" "Shuffle Family Guy in Flexarr" "Continue watching in Flexarr" "Add Severance to my watchlist in Flexarr" (see Watchlist) A show plays the episode you're up to. A film carries on from where you left off. Shuffle plays a show's episodes in a random order, one after another. Continue watching picks up whatever you were in the middle of most recently. #Podcasts "Play The Rest Is History in Flexarr" plays the episode you'd hear next "Play the latest The Rest Is History in Flexarr" plays the newest one you haven't heard "What's new in my podcasts in Flexarr" reads out the newest episodes, without opening anything "Add The Rest Is History to Up Next in Flexarr" "Play my Up Next in Flexarr" These work for podcasts the profile follows. See Podcasts. #Controlling what's playing "Pause Flexarr" "Resume Flexarr" "Stop Flexarr" "Turn on night mode in Flexarr" (and "Turn off night mode in Flexarr"). If night mode is on a schedule and already doing what you asked, the schedule stays; otherwise Siri says it replaced the schedule. #Playing on your Apple TV By default, what you ask for plays on the iPhone or iPad you asked. To send it to an Apple TV instead: On the iPhone or iPad, open Flexarr and go to Settings › Siri. Under Siri plays on, choose the Apple TV. Now "Play the next episode of Severance in Flexarr" starts it on the TV, and Siri tells you where it's playing. Pause, resume and stop go to the same TV. You can also name a device as you ask, for example "… on the living room TV". The name is the one the device has in Flexarr's list of signed-in devices. Important The Apple TV only takes commands while Flexarr is open on it. If it isn't, Siri says so, and what you asked for starts if you open Flexarr on the TV within two minutes. Siri isn't limited to Apple TVs: any iPhone or iPad signed in to your server can be chosen in the same way, as long as Flexarr is open on it. #Siri on the Apple TV itself The Apple TV app carries the same actions for the Siri Remote, but it hasn't been confirmed that tvOS passes these requests to apps like Flexarr. For now, the dependable way is to ask your iPhone or iPad. #The Shortcuts app Everything Siri can do is also in the Shortcuts app on iPhone and iPad, as actions you can put together yourself or run from an automation. Search for Flexarr when adding an action. You'll find: Action What it does Play a film or show Plays a film, or the next episode of a show. Can start from the beginning. Shuffle a show Plays a show's episodes in a random order. Continue watching Picks up what you were in the middle of. Add to watchlist Puts a film or show from your library on your watchlist. Pause, resume or stop Controls what Flexarr is playing. Night mode Turns night mode on or off, here or on another device with Flexarr open. Dialogue boost Sets dialogue boost to off, low, medium or high, here or on another device with Flexarr open. Play a podcast's latest episode The newest episode you haven't heard. What's new in my podcasts Says the newest episodes you haven't heard. Add a podcast to Up Next Puts the next episode at the end of Up Next. Play Up Next Plays your podcast queue from the start. Search Flexarr Opens the app on a search. The play and control actions have an On setting, where you choose this device or another one signed in to your server. That's handy for a shortcut of your own. A "Film night" shortcut could use Apple's own actions to dim the lights and wake the Apple TV, open Flexarr on it, then use Play a film or show with On set to that TV. Play a film o

title: Notifications and widgets
description: Get told on your iPhone or iPad when something new is ready, add podcast widgets to your Home Screen, and fill the Apple TV's Top Shelf.
text: Flexarr can tell your phone when something new arrives, keep podcasts on your Home Screen and Lock Screen, and put what you're watching at the top of the Apple TV's Home screen. #Notifications (iPhone and iPad) #Turn them on In the Flexarr app, go to Settings › Notifications. Turn on Notifications, and allow them when iOS asks. Under Tell me about, choose what you want to hear about. Tap Send test notification to check one arrives. If iOS has notifications switched off for Flexarr, the page says so and offers Open Settings to allow them there first. #What you can be told about Films and Shows: something new in the library that you haven't seen, in a library your profile can see. A brand-new show says so, and several episodes of one show arriving together are one notification. Upgrades and replacements of things you already have don't count. Podcasts: a new episode of a show you follow. Recordings: a Live TV recording has finished. This appears when Live TV is set up. Requests: something you asked for through Flexarr is ready. This takes the place of the ordinary "new" notification for it. Upcoming (off to start with): each morning, at the hour you choose under At, what's airing or out today from the shows you watch and the films you asked for. A library's first scan never notifies, and a big batch arriving at once is summed up in one notification, so adding a new library or a season pack won't flood your phone. Notifications have buttons. Films and episodes have Play, Download and Play on Apple TV. Podcast episodes have Play and Download. Tapping the notification opens the title. #One profile per phone Each phone gets notifications for one profile: the one it was on when you turned them on. A phone the household shares gets one set, not one for each person. If you switch profile, Settings › Notifications offers Get notifications for … instead. See Profiles. Signing the phone out, or signing it out from Settings › Security on the web, stops its notifications. #How they reach your phone, and what's shared Apple only delivers notifications that come from the app maker's own key, and that key can't be handed to every Flexarr server. So your server sends each notification through a small relay at flexarr.io, which hands it to Apple to deliver. Here's what goes where: When you turn notifications on, your phone makes a random secret key and gives it to your own server. It never leaves the two of them. When something new arrives, your server writes the notification (title, text, artwork link and buttons) and encrypts it with that key. Your server sends the relay the encrypted notification and your phone's Apple push address. The relay can't read the notification, and keeps nothing. The relay passes it to Apple under a plain "Something new is ready" message. On your phone, Flexarr decrypts it and shows the real title, text, artwork and buttons. So the relay and Apple see that your phone got a notification, and when, but not what it says. Artwork in a notification is a public poster address, which your phone fetches to show it. The one exception is the Lock Screen panel for a TV you're following. Apple reads its updates directly, so they can't be encrypted: they carry only whether the TV is paused, how far in it is, how long it is and its speed. The title and picture are put there by your phone and never pass through the relay. The privacy policy has the details. Note A server can use no relay at all. Set the environment variable Flexarr__Notifications__Enabled=false (or Flexarr:Notifications:Enabled set to false in the server's settings) and restart. The app then says your server has notifications turned off. #Widgets (iPhone and iPad) Flexarr has three widgets. Add them the usual way: touch and hold an empty part of the Home Screen, tap Edit › Add Widget, and search for Flexarr. Continue listening shows the episode you're on, with a play and pause button. Small and medium sizes for the Home Screen, and a Lock Screen size too. Up Next

title: Home Assistant
description: Add Flexarr to Home Assistant so every Apple TV, iPhone and iPad becomes a media player, and dim the lights when a film starts.
text: Home Assistant is a popular app for running your smart home yourself. Flexarr has an integration for it, so your home can react to what you're watching: lights down when a film starts, up again when the credits roll. The integration lives in its own repository, flexarr-home-assistant, and needs Flexarr 0.45.0 or later. #What you get A media player for each device. Every Apple TV, iPhone and iPad signed in to Flexarr appears in Home Assistant, named as it is in Flexarr's list of signed-in devices. It shows what's playing (title, show, season and episode, artwork and position) and has play, pause and stop. It's idle while Flexarr is open with nothing playing, and off when Flexarr isn't open on it. Devices you connect later appear by themselves. Device triggers for started, paused, resumed, credits, ended and stopped, to pick in an automation's Device trigger. A flexarr_playback event for every change, which covers browsers too. #Install it The easiest way is through HACS, the community store for Home Assistant, which also tells you about updates. In Home Assistant, open HACS, then the ⋮ menu, then Custom repositories. Add https://github.com/danleach-glitch/flexarr-home-assistant with the type Integration. Find Flexarr in HACS, download it, and restart Home Assistant. Go to Settings › Devices & services › Add integration and choose Flexarr. Enter the Server address, for example http://192.168.1.20:8383, and the API key. The API key is in Flexarr under Settings › Security, signed in as the main profile. Showing it asks for the admin PIN. Note If you copied the integration into custom_components by hand before it had its own repository, it keeps working. Remove the old copy and install it through HACS to get updates. #Play something from Home Assistant Call media_player.play_media with a Flexarr title's id. You'll find the id in the title's address in the web app. A show's id plays the episode that device's profile is up to. action: media_player.play_media target: entity_id: media_player.living_room_tv data: media_content_id: 01a17ab1-0000-0000-0000-000000000000 media_content_type: tvshow As with Siri, Flexarr has to be open on the device for it to play. #The playback event flexarr_playback carries: Field What it is type started, paused, resumed, credits, ended or stopped device_id the Home Assistant device (none for a browser) device_name the device or browser, as named in Flexarr profile whose profile is watching media_type movie, episode, music or podcast title, series_title, season, episode what's playing media_id its Flexarr id position, duration in seconds Credits fires where Flexarr has found the end credits, within about ten seconds of them starting. A title without credits found goes straight to ended. See Subtitles and skipping for how credits are found. A playback that stops reporting counts as stopped after two minutes, or fifteen if it was paused. #Example: lights down for films This dims the living room when a film starts on the living room TV, and brings the lights up at the credits or when you stop. automation: - alias: Lights down for a film triggers: - trigger: event event_type: flexarr_playback event_data: type: started media_type: movie device_name: Living room TV actions: - action: light.turn_on target: { entity_id: light.living_room } data: { brightness_pct: 10, transition: 5 } - alias: Lights up at the credits triggers: - trigger: event event_type: flexarr_playback event_data: { type: credits, device_name: Living room TV } - trigger: event event_type: flexarr_playback event_data: { type: stopped, device_name: Living room TV } actions: - action: light.turn_on target: { entity_id: light.living_room } data: { brightness_pct: 80, transition: 10 } Change Living room TV to your device's name in Flexarr, and light.living_room to your own light. Tip Leave out media_type: movie to dim the lights for episodes too, or add a profile to make it only happen when you're the one watching. #For other automation tools The inte

title: Use an AI assistant
description: Connect Claude or another AI assistant to Flexarr over MCP, so it can search your library, see what's playing and play things on your TV.
text: Flexarr is an MCP server. MCP (the Model Context Protocol) is a standard way for AI assistants such as Claude to use other apps. Connect one to Flexarr and you can ask it things like "What am I in the middle of?", "Put the next Traitors on the living room TV" or "Queue the new Rest Is History episodes". #What an assistant can do Tool What it does search_library Finds films, shows and episodes by title. continue_watching What you're in the middle of, most recent first. next_up The episode to watch next in a show. list_devices The Apple TVs, iPhones and iPads signed in, whether Flexarr is open on each, and what each is playing. now_playing Everything playing right now on every screen: which device, whose profile, what, and how far in. play_on_device Plays a title on a device. A show plays the episode you're up to; it can shuffle a show or start from the beginning. control_device Pauses, resumes or stops a device. set_device_sound Changes a device's dialogue boost, night mode or speakers, while Flexarr is open on it. mark_watched Marks a film or episode watched or unwatched; a show or season marks every episode. Unwatched also forgets how far in it was, taking it out of Continue Watching. remove_from_continue_watching Takes a film or episode out of Continue Watching without marking it watched. A show stays out until you play another episode of it. watchlist Your watchlist, with whether each title is ready to play, on its way, coming out later, or not available. add_to_watchlist Adds a film or show to your watchlist: one from your library, or any title by name (that needs Seerr). Says if it was requested too. remove_from_watchlist Takes a title off your watchlist. It doesn't cancel a request. podcasts The podcasts you follow, with how many episodes you haven't heard. new_podcast_episodes The newest episodes you haven't heard. podcast_up_next Your podcast Up Next queue. add_to_up_next Queues an episode, at the end or to play next. live_channels Live TV channels with what's on now and next. watch_channel_on_device Puts a channel on a device. record_programme Sets a programme, or every showing of a series, to record. recordings What's set to record, and what's been recorded. The Live TV tools are only useful once Live TV is set up. See Live TV. As with Siri, a device only plays what it's told while Flexarr is open on it. If it isn't, the command waits two minutes for Flexarr to be opened there, and the assistant is told so. The assistant acts as the main profile, since it signs in with the API key. Its Continue Watching, podcasts and marks are the main profile's. #What you'll need Your server's address, such as http://mini.local:8383 or http://192.168.1.20:8383. The MCP address is that with /api/v1/mcp on the end. The API key, from Settings › Security in Flexarr, signed in as the main profile. Showing it asks for the admin PIN. #Claude Code In a terminal, run: claude mcp add --transport http flexarr http://mini.local:8383/api/v1/mcp --header "X-Api-Key: <your key>" Change mini.local to your server's name or address, and <your key> to the API key. Then start Claude Code and ask it something about your library. #Other assistants Any MCP client that can connect to a server over HTTP (sometimes called "Streamable HTTP") and send a header can use Flexarr. Give it: URL: http://<server>:8383/api/v1/mcp Header: X-Api-Key with your API key The exact place to enter these differs from app to app, so check your assistant's own help for adding an MCP server. Some apps, including Claude Desktop's configuration file, only start MCP servers as local programs. For those, a small bridge program that forwards to an HTTP server, such as mcp-remote, can connect them to Flexarr's address with the header. Follow the bridge's own instructions; note that some bridges insist on https:// unless told otherwise. Note Assistants that connect from the vendor's cloud, rather than from your own computer, can't reach a server on your home network. Use an assistant th

title: Bring your history over from Plex
description: Copy what each person has watched, and where they stopped, from Plex Media Server into Flexarr, matched by file and without changing Plex.
text: If you've been using Plex Media Server, Flexarr can copy across what you've watched and where you stopped, so Continue Watching and the watched ticks pick up where you left off. Plex itself is never changed: Flexarr takes a private copy of Plex's database, reads it, and deletes the copy. #What comes over Watched films and episodes, with how many times each was played. Resume points for anything part-watched, so it shows in Continue Watching. Profile pictures, if you use Plex Home (a separate button, below). Each Plex user's history goes into the Flexarr profile you choose, so the household's histories stay apart. #What doesn't Music. Only films and episodes are brought over. Files Flexarr doesn't have. Titles are matched by the file on disk, not by name. If a file Plex knows about isn't in one of your Flexarr libraries, it's skipped and counted in the summary. Anything else in Plex: playlists, collections, ratings, server settings and users. Create profiles in Flexarr yourself (Profiles). #Before you start Flexarr reads Plex's database file, com.plexapp.plugins.library.db, so it has to be able to see it. Plex on the same computer. Flexarr looks in the usual places on a Mac, on Linux and on Windows, and normally finds it without help. Plex in Docker, or Flexarr in Docker. Make Plex's data folder visible to Flexarr, for example by mounting it into Flexarr's container read-only, then give Flexarr the full path to the database file when it asks. The file sits in Plex's data folder under Plug-in Support/Databases/. Plex on a different computer. Copy its Plug-in Support/Databases folder to the Flexarr machine and point Flexarr at the copied com.plexapp.plugins.library.db. Note Flexarr only accepts a path to a file named com.plexapp.plugins.library.db. It won't read any other file you point it at. Matching is by file path, so your libraries need to be set up in Flexarr first, with their scans finished. If Plex saw your media under different paths from Flexarr (common when one of them runs in Docker), add a path mapping in Settings › Connections › Media folders before importing; Flexarr applies the same mappings to Plex's paths. See Media paths. #Bring the history over You need the main profile for this. In the web app, open Settings › Libraries and choose Bring over from Plex. Flexarr says where it found Plex. If it says Plex wasn't found, type the full path to com.plexapp.plugins.library.db and choose Look there. Under Whose history, pick the Plex user. Each is listed with how many titles they've watched and how many are in progress. If you have more than one Flexarr profile, choose one under Into which Flexarr profile. It starts on the main profile. Choose Bring history over. When it's done, a summary says how many titles were matched, how many are now watched, and how many are ready to resume. It also says how many files Plex knows about that aren't in your Flexarr libraries. Repeat steps 3 to 5 for each person, picking their Plex user and their Flexarr profile each time. #Running it again is safe You can run the import as often as you like. For each title, the most recent viewing wins: if you've watched something in Flexarr since you last watched it in Plex, Flexarr keeps its own, and the summary tells you how many were left alone. Play counts never go down. This makes it easy to try Flexarr alongside Plex for a while and bring over whatever you've watched in Plex in the meantime. Tip If a lot of files come up as not matched, check your path mappings, then rescan the libraries and run the import again. #Profile pictures Under the import there's a Profile pictures panel. Use Plex profile pictures takes each Plex Home user's picture and puts it on the Flexarr profile with the same name, replacing any picture it has. Plex's owner is matched to the main profile if no profile shares their name. This step does go online: Flexarr reads Plex's own sign-in from its settings file and makes one request to plex.tv for the list of Home users

title: Library health
description: Find spare copies and the space they use, files that can't be read, standard-definition films and wrong matches, and fix them with Sonarr and Radarr.
text: Library health is a check-up for your films and TV. It shows what's wrong, how much space spare copies take, and a button to fix each problem, usually by asking Sonarr or Radarr to do the work. Open it in the web app from Settings › Libraries › Library health, as the main profile. The Overview page in Settings links to it too. #The health score At the top is a score out of 100: the share of your films and episodes with nothing wrong. Next to it is a breakdown of what's affecting the rest, such as spare copies, unreadable files or missing artwork. Groups with nothing in them are left out, and a line underneath says what's all clear ("every title has a single copy", "every film has an HD copy"). #Spare copies Sometimes a film or episode ends up with more than one file: an upgrade that didn't replace the old one, or the same file in two folders. Spare copies lists each one, how many copies it has and how much space the spares use. The total you'd free is in the group's description. Remove spares on a title deletes its extra files. Remove all spare copies does the whole list, after asking first, with a progress bar. Flexarr always keeps two copies safe: the best one (highest quality), and the one Sonarr or Radarr are tracking. Usually they're the same file. When they're not, both stay and the summary tells you; open the title's row to see each copy with its resolution, codec and size, and use Delete this copy on the one you don't want. Copies that are the same file twice are marked Identical. Important Removing spares deletes files from your disk. It can't be undone. #Run a health check The Health check panel looks at every file: whether it's still on disk, whether it's empty, and whether it can be read. Choose Run health check and it works through your library in the background, with a progress bar. Problems are listed under Missing from disk, Empty files and Still unreadable, each with Search again to have Sonarr or Radarr fetch it again. #Files that can't be read Files Flexarr couldn't open when it scanned them are listed under Files that can't be read, with the reason. This is usually a damaged or unfinished download. Get a new copy asks Sonarr or Radarr to search for the title again; a fresh copy fixes playback. #Standard-definition films Only in standard definition lists films whose best copy is below 720p. Find a better copy asks Radarr to search for the film again, so it can upgrade it within the quality profile you've set in Radarr. When Sonarr or Radarr are already fetching a new copy, the row shows how far along it is ("Downloading 45%") instead of the button. #Check these matches Films and shows that Sonarr and Radarr don't manage get their details by searching for the folder's name. That can find the wrong title: an older show with the same name, or a remake. They're listed under Check these matches. If a match is right, choose Ignore. It leaves the list and stays as it is. If it's wrong, choose Fix match (below). #Missing artwork Titles with no poster or details are listed under Missing artwork. Artwork comes from Radarr and Sonarr, so if they aren't connected, connect them in Settings › Connections (Connect Sonarr, Radarr, Lidarr and Seerr). If they are, the title wasn't found: fix its match, or rename its folder to the form Title (Year) and rescan. #Fix match Fix match puts right a film or show that's been matched to the wrong title. It's on each row in Check these matches and Missing artwork, and in the ⋯ menu on any film's or show's page (main profile only). Choose Fix match. The dialog shows the full path of the film's files, or the show's folder, so you can see what's being matched. Search for the right title. Try the title as it was first released, or add the year. Pick it. Each result says whether it's the Current match, already in Sonarr or Radarr, or would be added to them. Flexarr keeps your choice through every later refresh. title: Backups
description: How Flexarr backs itself up every night, where backups are kept, and how to restore one or move your settings to another server.
headings: Restore or import from a file
text: Your films, shows and music live on your own drives, and Flexarr can always scan them again. What it can't rebuild is everything you've added on top: profiles, what everyone has watched, playlists, collections, settings and signed-in devices. That's what a backup holds. Everything here is in the web app under Settings › Backup and restore, as the main profile. #What's in a backup Profiles, with their PINs and pictures What every profile has watched, and where they stopped Playlists, collections, podcast follows and other per-profile data The server's settings and keys (config.json) Signed-in browsers, phones and TVs Artwork, subtitles and scrubbing previews are left out. They come back by themselves. Your media files and logs aren't included either. #Automatic backups Flexarr makes a backup every night at half past three and keeps the last 7. If the server was off overnight, it catches up a few minutes after it next starts. It also makes one before an upgrade changes the database, and before a restore, so you can always go back. The last 3 of each of those are kept. Backups you make by hand are never deleted automatically. To stop the nightly backups, turn off Back up every night under Automatic backups. We don't recommend it. #Back up now Choose Back up now at any time, for example before changing a lot of settings. Each backup in the list shows when it was made, why (Nightly, Made by hand, Before an upgrade, Before a restore), its size and the Flexarr version. #Where backups are kept The list says where: Kept in and the folder. By default that's a backups folder inside Flexarr's data folder: Install Default backups folder Mac ~/.flexarr/data/backups Docker /config/backups inside the container, so wherever you mapped /config A backup on the same drive as Flexarr won't help if that drive fails. To keep them elsewhere, type another folder under Automatic backups › Folder and choose Save: a second drive, or a network share mounted on the server. In Docker, the folder has to be one you've mapped into the container. Leave it empty to go back to the data folder. If the chosen folder isn't there when a backup is due (a drive that's unplugged, or a share that didn't mount), Flexarr says so on the page rather than quietly filling up its own drive. #Download a backup Use the Download icon on a backup to save a copy to your computer. You can protect it with a passphrase of at least 8 characters. The file holds your server's keys and the passwords for Sonarr, Radarr and the like, so either set a passphrase or keep the file somewhere private. Tip Flexarr asks for the passphrase when you open the file later. Keep it in a password manager. #Restore a backup Restoring puts the whole server back to how it was when the backup was made: profiles, what's been watched, settings, keys and sign-ins. Anything since is lost. Find the backup in the list and use its Restore icon. To restore a file you downloaded, use From a file further down the page instead (below). Read the warning, and enter the admin PIN if it has one. Choose Restore and restart. Flexarr first makes a copy of the server as it is now (it appears in the list as Before a restore), so you can change your mind. It then restarts to put the backup in place. Anyone watching is stopped. The page reloads when Flexarr is back. Before anything changes, the backup is checked. A damaged one, one made by a newer version of Flexarr, or a file that isn't a Flexarr backup is refused. This machine's own paths (ffmpeg and the cache) are kept as they are. Important Flexarr stops itself to finish a restore and relies on whatever runs it to start it again. The Mac install does this. In Docker, the container needs a restart policy such as --restart unless-stopped (or restart: unless-stopped in Compose).
